ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations of Endocrine:
Overview — Hypothalamic-Pituitary Axes
The hypothalamus and pituitary form the central control hub of the endocrine system — the hypothalamus integrates signals from the brain and body and directs the pituitary, which in turn controls the peripheral endocrine glands.
The organising principle: most hormones are controlled by an axis — hypothalamus → pituitary → target gland → hormone — regulated by negative feedback (the final hormone switches off the levels above it). Almost every endocrine disease and test is understood by asking "where in the axis is the problem, and which way is the feedback going?"
Why it matters: this single framework explains primary vs secondary endocrine disease, why we measure paired hormones (e.g. TSH + T4), dynamic testing (suppression/stimulation), and steroid HPA suppression — cross-ref the individual axes (thyroid, adrenal, etc.) and the clinical endocrine notes.

The prolactin exception (high-yield): prolactin is unique — it is under tonic inhibition by dopamine (the hypothalamus suppresses it by default). So anything that interrupts the pituitary stalk (tumour, compression) → loss of dopamine inhibition → ↑prolactin ("stalk effect"); and dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) → ↑prolactin.
TRH also stimulates prolactin → why primary hypothyroidism (high TRH) can cause mild hyperprolactinaemia.
Negative Feedback — the key to everything
The loop: the final hormone (e.g. cortisol, T4) feeds back to suppress the hypothalamus + pituitary → keeps levels stable. e.g. ↑cortisol → ↓CRH + ↓ACTH (cortisol controls its own production).
The diagnostic logic (highest-yield payoff) — feedback tells you where the problem is via the paired hormones:
Pattern Interpretation
Low target + HIGH pituitaryPrimary gland failure (gland can't respond; pituitary shouting louder) — e.g. ↓T4 + ↑TSH = primary hypothyroidism
Low target + LOW/normal pituitarySecondary (pituitary) failure (pituitary not driving it) — e.g. ↓T4 + ↓TSH = secondary hypothyroidism
High target + LOW pituitaryPrimary gland overactivity (feedback suppressing pituitary) — e.g. ↑T4 + ↓TSH = primary hyperthyroidism
High target + HIGH pituitaryPituitary-driven (secondary) overactivity — e.g. ↑cortisol + ↑ACTH = Cushing's disease (pituitary)
This is why endocrine tests measure hormones in pairs (TSH + T4, ACTH + cortisol, LH/FSH + sex steroids) — the combination localises the lesion to gland vs pituitary.
Dynamic Testing — the clever application of feedback (high-yield)
When a single measurement is ambiguous, you manipulate the axis and watch the response:
Suppression tests — for suspected OVERproduction
  • Give something that should switch the axis off; failure to suppress = autonomous overproduction
  • e.g. dexamethasone suppression test (Cushing's), oral glucose tolerance test (acromegaly)
Stimulation tests — for suspected UNDERproduction
  • Give the stimulating hormone; failure to respond = gland can't produce
  • e.g. Short Synacthen test (ACTH → cortisol, for Addison's)
The principle: suppress when you suspect too much, stimulate when you suspect too little — the unifying logic of endocrine dynamic tests.
The Posterior Pituitary — the two stored hormones
  • ADH (vasopressin): made in the hypothalamus, stored/released posteriorly → acts on the renal collecting duct (water reabsorption) — cross-ref renal/BP regulation; too little = diabetes insipidus, too much = SIADH
  • Oxytocin: uterine contraction (labour) + milk ejection (let-down reflex)

Overview — Thyroid Physiology & the Thyroid Axis
The thyroid produces hormones that set the body's basal metabolic rate — influencing nearly every tissue's metabolism, growth, and (in children) development.
The organising principle: this is the TRH → TSH → T3/T4 axis (a specific instance of the hypothalamic-pituitary framework), governed by negative feedback — and the TSH + T4 pairing is the single most useful endocrine test, decoding hypo/hyperthyroidism into primary vs secondary.
Why it matters: the normal axis explains why TSH is the key screening test, the primary-vs-secondary patterns, why thyroid disease affects metabolism so widely, and how antithyroid drugs work — cross-ref the hypothalamic-pituitary axes subtab, hypo/hyperthyroidism, clinical thyroid notes.

Negative feedback: T3/T4 suppress both TRH and TSH → keeps levels stable (the loop that makes TSH such a sensitive test).
Thyroid Hormone Synthesis — the iodine story
The thyroid follicular cells make hormone in steps (the basis of where antithyroid drugs act):
  • Iodide trapping: iodide pumped into the follicular cell (Na⁺/I⁻ symporter)
  • Oxidation + organification: thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidises iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin → forms MIT + DIT
  • Coupling: MIT + DIT combine → T3 (3 iodines) and T4 (4 iodines), stored bound to thyroglobulin in the colloid
  • Release: TSH stimulates release of T3/T4 into the blood
Iodine is essential (it is literally in the hormone) → iodine deficiency → goitre/hypothyroidism (the commonest cause worldwide).
The drug link (high-yield): carbimazole/propylthiouracil block TPO (→ ↓synthesis); PTU also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion — cross-ref hyperthyroidism treatment.
T4 vs T3 — the prohormone concept (high-yield)
T4 (thyroxine) T3 (triiodothyronine)
Amount made by thyroid~90% (main secreted form)~10%
ActivityLess active (a prohormone)The active hormone (~4× more potent)
ConversionConverted to T3 peripherally (in tissues, by deiodinase)The active product
Half-lifeLong (~7 days)Short
The key concept: the thyroid mostly secretes T4, converted to the active T3 in peripheral tissues → T4 is essentially a circulating prohormone/reservoir (its long half-life is why levothyroxine [T4] is the treatment — stable, once-daily).
Most thyroid hormone is protein-bound (to thyroxine-binding globulin) → only the free fraction is active (why we measure free T4/T3).
Actions of Thyroid Hormone — why it affects everything
Thyroid hormone acts on nuclear receptors in nearly all tissues → ↑metabolic rate:

Metabolic rate↑basal metabolic rate, ↑O₂ consumption, ↑heat production
Cardiovascular↑heart rate + contractility (↑β-adrenergic sensitivity)
CNS/developmentEssential for brain development (deficiency in infancy → cretinism); ↑alertness
GrowthNeeded for normal growth (with GH)
Metabolism↑glucose, fat, protein turnover
Gut/other↑gut motility
The unifying idea: thyroid hormone sets the "metabolic thermostat" → hyperthyroidism = everything sped up (weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, anxiety, diarrhoea) and hypothyroidism = everything slowed (weight gain, bradycardia, cold intolerance, lethargy, constipation) — the symptoms are derivable from the physiology, not memorised.

Overview — Adrenal Physiology & the HPA Axis
The adrenal glands sit atop the kidneys and have two functionally separate parts: the cortex (steroid hormones) and the medulla (catecholamines) — different embryological origins, control, and products.
The organising principle: the cortex is organised into three zones, each making a different steroid class, and the cortisol arm is controlled by the HPA axis (CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with negative feedback). Understanding the zones + the axis explains Addison's, Cushing's, Conn's, and steroid therapy.
Why it matters: underpins adrenal insufficiency/crisis, Cushing's, Conn's, phaeochromocytoma, and steroid HPA suppression/sick-day rules — cross-ref the hypothalamic-pituitary axes subtab, steroid equivalents & sick-day rules, BP regulation (aldosterone/RAAS), clinical adrenal notes.

The key control distinction (high-yield): cortisol + androgens are ACTH-driven, but aldosterone is primarily RAAS-driven (angiotensin II + potassium), not ACTH. This is why in secondary adrenal insufficiency (↓ACTH) aldosterone is preserved (RAAS still works), whereas in primary (Addison's) both are lost.
The HPA Axis (cortisol) — the framework applied
  • CRH (hypothalamus) → ACTH (pituitary) → cortisol (zona fasciculata), with cortisol negative feedback on CRH + ACTH
  • Diurnal rhythm: cortisol peaks in the early morning, troughs at night (why cortisol is measured at 9am, and why timing matters in testing)
  • Stress response: physical/psychological stress → ↑CRH/ACTH → ↑cortisol (the body's stress hormone) — the basis of sick-day rules: a stressed body needs more cortisol

The clinical logic (derivable disease): excess cortisol (Cushing's) = ↑glucose (diabetes), ↑BP, central obesity, immunosuppression, osteoporosis, thin skin, mood change; deficiency (Addison's) = ↓glucose, ↓BP, fatigue, weight loss — the features fall straight out of the physiology.
The therapeutic-steroid link: the anti-inflammatory action is why steroids are used as drugs — chronic use → HPA suppression (exogenous cortisol suppresses CRH/ACTH → adrenal atrophy) → cannot mount a stress response → sick-day rules + cannot stop abruptly (cross-ref steroid note).
Aldosterone — the mineralocorticoid (the RAAS link)
  • Made in the zona glomerulosa, controlled by RAAS (angiotensin II) + potassium (cross-ref BP regulation)
  • Action: acts on the renal collecting duct → ↑Na⁺ reabsorption + ↑K⁺ and H⁺ excretion → ↑blood volume/BP (cross-ref nephron)
The clinical logic: excess (Conn's / primary hyperaldosteronism) = hypertension + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis; deficiency (part of Addison's) = hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypotension — derivable from the Na⁺-retaining/K⁺-excreting action.
The Adrenal Medulla — catecholamines (the sympathetic gland)
  • Modified sympathetic ganglion → secretes adrenaline (~80%) + noradrenaline directly into the blood in response to sympathetic stimulation (the "fight or flight" hormonal arm)
  • Actions: ↑heart rate + contractility, vasoconstriction, bronchodilation, ↑glucose, pupil dilation — the systemic sympathetic response
  • The clinical link: phaeochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting medullary tumour) → episodic hypertension, palpitations, sweating, headache — derivable from excess catecholamines (cross-ref)

Overview — Glucose Homeostasis (Insulin & Glucagon)
Blood glucose is kept within a narrow range (~4–7 mmol/L) because the brain depends on a constant glucose supply, while sustained high glucose damages tissues — regulated chiefly by the opposing hormones insulin and glucagon from the pancreas.
The organising principle: glucose homeostasis is a balance between insulin (the only hormone that lowers glucose) and its counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline, GH, which raise it) — and the fed vs fasted state determines which dominates.
Why it matters: the physiology behind diabetes (type 1 vs 2), DKA, hypoglycaemia, and every diabetes drug — cross-ref metabolism notes (glycolysis/gluconeogenesis), the fed/fasted state, diabetes, DKA, clinical endocrine notes.
The Pancreatic Islets — the endocrine pancreas
The islets of Langerhans (the endocrine pancreas, ~1–2% of pancreatic mass) contain:
Cell Hormone Effect on glucose
β (beta) cellsInsulinLOWERS glucose (the only hormone that does)
α (alpha) cellsGlucagonRAISES glucose
δ (delta) cellsSomatostatinInhibits both (+ other hormones)
The key asymmetry (high-yield): there are many hormones that raise glucose (glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline, GH — "counter-regulatory") but only insulin lowers it → this is why insulin deficiency (diabetes) is so impactful, and why hypoglycaemia is dangerous (redundant defences against high glucose, single defence against low).
Insulin — the storage/anabolic hormone
  • Trigger: released by β cells in response to ↑blood glucose (also amino acids, incretins like GLP-1)
  • Overarching role: the "fed state" / anabolic / storage hormone — "fuel is plentiful, store it"
Tissue Insulin's action
Liver↑glycogen synthesis, ↓gluconeogenesis (stops making glucose)
Muscle↑glucose uptake (via GLUT4), ↑glycogen + protein synthesis
Adipose↑glucose uptake (GLUT4), ↑fat storage (lipogenesis), ↓lipolysis
Overall↓blood glucose; promotes storage of glucose, fat, protein
The GLUT4 point (high-yield): insulin causes GLUT4 glucose transporters to move to the cell surface in muscle + fat → glucose uptake. The brain and liver use insulin-independent transporters (GLUT1/2/3) → which is why the brain can still take up glucose without insulin (and why it is vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, not lack of insulin).
Mechanism: insulin binds a tyrosine kinase receptor → signalling cascade → GLUT4 translocation + enzyme effects.
Glucagon — the mobilising/catabolic hormone
  • Trigger: released by α cells in response to ↓blood glucose (fasting)
  • Role: the "fasted state" / catabolic / mobilising hormone — "fuel is low, release stores"
Tissue Glucagon's action
Liver↑glycogenolysis (break down glycogen) + ↑gluconeogenesis (make new glucose) → release glucose
Adipose↑lipolysis → free fatty acids + glycerol
Overall↑blood glucose + mobilises fat (→ ketones in prolonged fasting)
Glucagon acts mainly on the liver (the glucose factory + glycogen store).

Overview — Calcium Homeostasis (PTH & Vitamin D)
Blood calcium is kept in a tight range (~2.2–2.6 mmol/L) because calcium is critical for neuromuscular function, cardiac action potentials, clotting, and bone — controlled by PTH and vitamin D (raising calcium) opposed by calcitonin (minor).
The organising principle: calcium is regulated across three organs — bone, kidney, gut — and PTH is the master minute-to-minute controller, with vitamin D as its essential partner (especially for gut absorption). Phosphate moves in the opposite direction to calcium in much of this system.
Why it matters: underpins hyper/hypocalcaemia, primary/secondary hyperparathyroidism, CKD bone disease, vitamin D deficiency/osteomalacia, and the calcium clinical signs — cross-ref electrolytes (Ca²⁺), CKD bone disease, renal calculi, the nephron note, clinical bone/endocrine notes.
Why Calcium Matters + How It's Carried
  • Calcium is essential for: neuromuscular excitability (low Ca²⁺ → tetany; high Ca²⁺ → weakness), cardiac APs (the plateau — cross-ref), clotting (factor IV), bone, enzyme function
Carriage (high-yield): ~half is free (ionised) — the active fraction; the rest is bound (mainly to albumin). So total calcium must be "corrected" for albumin (low albumin → low total Ca²⁺ but normal ionised Ca²⁺).
pH effect: alkalosis ↑binding → ↓ionised Ca²⁺ → tetany (why hyperventilation causes peri-oral tingling/carpopedal spasm).

The phosphate point (high-yield): PTH raises calcium but LOWERS phosphate (↑renal phosphate excretion) → so primary hyperparathyroidism = ↑Ca²⁺ + ↓phosphate (a key diagnostic pattern).
The vitamin D link: PTH's effect on gut calcium is indirect — it works by stimulating the kidney to activate vitamin D, which then does the gut absorption.

Overview — Sex Hormones & the Reproductive Axes
The reproductive system is controlled by the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis — producing sex steroids that drive gamete production, secondary sexual characteristics, and (in females) the menstrual cycle.
The organising principle: the same axis — GnRH → LH/FSH → gonadal sex steroids — operates in both sexes, governed by negative feedback (with one crucial exception: the mid-cycle positive feedback that triggers ovulation). It is the hypothalamic-pituitary framework applied to the gonads.
Why it matters: underpins puberty, the menstrual cycle, contraception, infertility, PCOS, menopause, and hypogonadism — cross-ref the hypothalamic-pituitary axes subtab, the menstrual cycle (reproductive physiology), clinical O&G/endocrine notes.

The pulsatility point (high-yield): GnRH must be released in pulses — continuous GnRH paradoxically suppresses the axis (downregulates receptors). This is the basis of GnRH analogues used to suppress sex hormones (prostate cancer, endometriosis, precocious puberty).
Negative feedback: sex steroids + inhibin suppress GnRH/LH/FSH (the standard loop).

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidism:
Definition & The Decisive Fork

Hyperthyroidism = gland overproduces T3/T4. Thyrotoxicosis = clinical syndrome of excess thyroid hormone — the two are not synonyms. Thyrotoxicosis can occur without hyperthyroidism (e.g. thyroiditis leaking stored hormone).

Physiology anchor: TRH (hypothalamus) → TSH (anterior pituitary) → T3/T4 (thyroid). T3/T4 negative feedback suppresses TSH. Effects = ↑BMR + ↑catecholamine sensitivity (source of most signs).

The single decisive fork: High uptake on radioiodine scan = gland is making it (true hyperthyroidism — antithyroid drugs work). Low uptake = hormone is leaking from damage (thyrotoxicosis without hyperthyroidism — antithyroid drugs are useless here). Hold this distinction and the entire topic falls into place.
Subclinical hyperthyroidism: TSH suppressed + normal T3/T4. Often asymptomatic. Treat if TSH <0.1 with AF risk, osteoporosis, age >65, or cardiac disease.
Aetiology — Organised by the Uptake Fork
↑ Uptake — True Hyperthyroidism (gland making it)
  • Graves' disease — autoimmune; TSHR antibodies stimulate gland; most common cause; diffuse uptake
  • Toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's) — multiple autonomous nodules; patchy uptake
  • Solitary toxic adenoma — focal uptake
  • Amiodarone type I (Jod-Basedow) — iodine load drives excess synthesis
  • Secondary — pituitary TSH-secreting adenoma (rare; TSH paradoxically high)
  • β-hCG-driven — molar pregnancy, choriocarcinoma (hCG stimulates TSH receptor)
↓ Uptake — Leaking Hormone (not making it)
  • De Quervain's thyroiditis — viral; painful tender goitre; 3 phases: thyrotoxicosis → hypothyroid → recovery
  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis — transient early thyrotoxicosis (hashitoxicosis) before hypothyroidism
  • Postpartum thyroiditis — same 3-phase pattern; occurs 1–6 months post-delivery
  • Amiodarone type II — destructive thyroiditis; hormone leak
  • Excess levothyroxine — exogenous; TSH suppressed; gland not active
  • Struma ovarii — ectopic thyroid in ovarian teratoma
  • Metastatic follicular cancer — functioning ectopic tissue
Key implication: Antithyroid drugs (carbimazole, PTU) block thyroid synthesis — they only work in the high-uptake group. In thyroiditis/exogenous T4, there is nothing to block.
Clinical Features
General Thyrotoxicosis (catecholamine-driven — any cause)
  • Weight loss despite ↑ appetite
  • Heat intolerance, sweating
  • Tremor, anxiety, irritability, insomnia
  • Palpitations, tachycardia, AF
  • Diarrhoea
  • Oligomenorrhoea, reduced fertility
  • Proximal myopathy
  • Lid retraction + lid lag — sympathetic overstimulation of levator palpebrae; present in any thyrotoxicosis, not Graves'-specific
Graves'-Specific (TSHR antibody-driven — clinch the diagnosis)
  • Diffuse goitre + thyroid bruit — smooth, non-nodular; bruit from ↑ vascularity
  • Exophthalmos / proptosis — TSHR antibodies target retro-orbital tissue → GAG accumulation → eye protrudes; thyroid and orbit share TSH receptor
  • Pretibial myxoedema — waxy non-pitting oedema on shins; GAG deposits
  • Thyroid acropachy — finger clubbing + periosteal new bone; rarest feature
  • Smoking = main modifiable risk factor for Graves' eye disease
  • Associated autoimmune: pernicious anaemia, myasthenia gravis, T1DM

Management
1 — Symptom Control (all causes)
Propranolol (non-selective β-blocker) — blocks adrenergic symptoms (tremor, palpitations, tachycardia). Useful while awaiting thioamide effect and in thyroid storm. Does not treat the underlying cause.
2 — Antithyroid Drugs (high-uptake group only)
💊
Carbimazole — First-LineBlocks thyroid peroxidase (TPO) → ↓ T3/T4 synthesis. Benefit takes 10–20 days. Give for 12–18 months. Teratogenic (aplasia cutis) — avoid in pregnancy. Risk of pancreatitis.
↓
💊
Propylthiouracil (PTU) — Second-LineSame TPO block + inhibits peripheral T4→T3 conversion. Preferred in pregnancy (1st trimester) and carbimazole intolerance. Risk of hepatotoxicity.
↓
Agranulocytosis — Critical Safety PearlBoth thioamides can cause agranulocytosis (rare, life-threatening). Any sore throat → STOP drug immediately + urgent FBC. Warn all patients at initiation. Check baseline FBC + LFTs.
Two titration regimens: (1) Dose-titration — thioamide alone, adjusted to normalise TSH. (2) Block-and-replace — fixed high-dose thioamide to block all production + add levothyroxine to prevent hypothyroidism. Block-and-replace is avoided in pregnancy — use the lowest effective single antithyroid drug (dose-titration), as the antithyroid drug crosses the placenta but levothyroxine does not (fetal hypothyroidism/goitre risk).
3 — Definitive Treatment
Radioactive Iodine (RAI / I-131) — First-Line Definitive
  • First-line for Graves' disease and toxic MNG
  • Oral I-131 selectively taken up by thyroid → β-radiation destroys follicular cells
  • Remission takes 6–12 months; frequently leads to hypothyroidism (often desired endpoint)
  • CI: pregnancy, breastfeeding. Advise contraception for 6 months (women) / 4–6 months (men). Can worsen active Graves' eye disease — cover with steroids
Surgery — Thyroidectomy
  • Indicated if malignancy suspected, compressive goitre, RAI/drugs unsuitable, patient preference
  • Pre-op: euthyroid on thioamide first; give KI (potassium iodide) 10 days pre-op to reduce vascularity
  • Lifelong levothyroxine post-op
  • Complications: hypocalcaemia (parathyroid damage → check Ca²⁺ post-op) + recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (hoarse voice — check voice immediately)
🚨 Thyroid Storm

Life-threatening thyrotoxicosis. Precipitants: infection, surgery, iodine load, trauma, RAI. Features: fever >38.5°C, tachycardia/AF, confusion/delirium, vomiting. High mortality without treatment.

Four-arm bundle — hit every step of the pathway:
① Block synthesis — high-dose carbimazole 20–40mg 8-hourly (or PTU 200mg 4-hourly if preferred)
② Block release — potassium iodide (KI / Lugol's iodine) — given ≥1h after carbimazole (must block synthesis first or iodine will fuel more hormone)
③ Block conversion — hydrocortisone 100mg IV 6-hourly (inhibits peripheral T4→T3 conversion; also covers relative adrenal insufficiency)
④ Block effect — propranolol IV/oral (blocks adrenergic symptoms; reduces tachycardia/AF)
Plus: IV fluids, treat precipitant (antibiotics if sepsis), cooling, intensive care monitoring. Cholestyramine can bind thyroid hormone in gut (reduces enterohepatic recycling).

⭐ Exam Pearls

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidism:
Definition & The Decisive Fork

Hypothyroidism = underactive thyroid → insufficient T3/T4. Primary (95%) = thyroid gland pathology. Secondary (rare) = pituitary or hypothalamic failure to drive the gland.

The fork: Low T4 + HIGH TSH = primary (gland can't respond; pituitary compensates by pushing more TSH). Low T4 + low/normal TSH = secondary (pituitary not signalling; TSH absent or inappropriately low). This mirrors the hyperthyroidism fork in reverse — same axis, opposite direction.
Screening triggers: always check TFTs in new menorrhagia, infertility, hyperprolactinaemia, dyslipidaemia, depression, or carpal tunnel syndrome — hypothyroidism is the reversible cause behind all of these.
Aetiology — Organised by the Primary/Secondary Fork
Primary (High TSH) — Gland Pathology
  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis — commonest in developed world; autoimmune; anti-TPO + anti-thyroglobulin antibodies; can be goitrous or atrophic; associated MALT lymphoma risk
  • Iodine deficiency — commonest cause worldwide; endemic in mountainous regions; causes massive goitre
  • Iatrogenic: thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine (I-131), carbimazole/PTU (drug-induced)
  • Drugs: lithium (blocks thyroid hormone synthesis/release), amiodarone (can cause hypo or hyper — always check TFTs)
  • Riedel's thyroiditis — rare fibrous infiltration; hard fixed painless goitre; mimics malignancy
  • Congenital — thyroid agenesis/dyshormonogenesis; detected on neonatal Guthrie heel-prick screen
Secondary (Low/Normal TSH) — Pituitary/Hypothalamic
  • Pituitary adenoma / tumour compressing thyrotrophs
  • Sheehan's syndrome — post-partum pituitary necrosis after massive haemorrhage; classically failure to lactate + secondary hypothyroidism + adrenal insufficiency
  • Cranial radiotherapy — radiation damage to pituitary
  • Head trauma / surgery involving pituitary
  • Hypothalamic disease — low TRH → low TSH → low T4 (tertiary)
Hashimoto's autoimmune cluster: coeliac disease, T1DM, vitiligo, pernicious anaemia, Addison's disease. Amiodarone causes both hypo- and hyperthyroidism — a classic exam point in both thyroid notes.

  • Cold intolerance
  • Dry, coarse skin; hair loss (including outer third of eyebrows)
  • Constipation
  • Menorrhagia, infertility
  • Depression, cognitive slowing, poor memory
  • Hoarse, deep voice (myxoedema of vocal cords)
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome
Signs on Examination
  • Slow-relaxing tendon reflexes — the classic sign; opposite of brisk reflexes in hyperthyroidism
  • Bradycardia
  • Periorbital puffiness, non-pitting oedema, effusions (pleural/pericardial/ascites)
  • Puffy doughy skin (myxoedema)
  • Goitre (Hashimoto's, iodine deficiency)
  • Loss of outer eyebrow (classic exam feature)
  • Macroglossia

The fork: low T4 + high TSH = primary (gland). Low T4 + low/normal TSH = secondary (pituitary). Always ask which direction TSH goes.
Hashimoto's = commonest in developed world (anti-TPO). Iodine deficiency = commonest worldwide. Hashimoto's cluster: coeliac, T1DM, vitiligo, pernicious anaemia.
Slow-relaxing reflexes + loss of outer eyebrow + ↑CK + ↓Na + ↑lipids = the classic hypothyroid discriminators. Brisk reflexes = hyperthyroid (same axis, opposite direction).

Amiodarone causes both hypo- and hyperthyroidism (contains 37% iodine). Lithium causes hypothyroidism. Sheehan's = post-partum pituitary necrosis → secondary hypothyroidism.
Congenital hypothyroidism: detected on Guthrie heel-prick test (day 5–8). Untreated → cretinism (irreversible intellectual disability). Early T4 treatment is curative.
ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syndrome:
Definition, Fork & Physiology

Cushing's syndrome = clinical state of excess glucocorticoid — any cause. Cushing's disease = specifically a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma. The two are not synonyms — a classic exam trap.

The ACTH fork: measure plasma ACTH. High ACTH = ACTH-dependent (source is making ACTH — pituitary or ectopic). Suppressed/low ACTH = ACTH-independent (adrenal making cortisol autonomously; ACTH suppressed by feedback). This single result directs all imaging and further testing.

Cortisol physiology anchor: CRH (hypothalamus) → ACTH (anterior pituitary) → cortisol (adrenal cortex). Cortisol has a diurnal rhythm — highest in the morning, lowest at midnight (loss of this rhythm is the basis of late-night salivary cortisol and dex suppression tests). Effects: gluconeogenesis, protein catabolism, immune suppression, mineralocorticoid-like actions.

Aetiology — Organised by the ACTH Fork
↑ ACTH — ACTH-Dependent
  • Cushing's disease — pituitary adenoma secreting ACTH → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia; commonest endogenous cause
  • Ectopic ACTH — SCLC most common; also carcinoid, phaeochromocytoma; very high ACTH; rapid onset; marked pigmentation + hypokalaemia; often no classic body habitus (no time to develop)
↓ ACTH — ACTH-Independent
  • Iatrogenic steroids — long-term prednisolone/dexamethasone; commonest cause overall
  • Adrenal adenoma — unilateral adrenal mass; ACTH suppressed by autonomous cortisol
  • Adrenal carcinoma — often larger mass; may co-secrete androgens (virilisation)
  • Carney complex — rare; ACTH-independent bilateral nodular hyperplasia + cardiac myxoma
The two "commonest" facts: iatrogenic = commonest overall; Cushing's disease = commonest endogenous. Both appear in exams.
Pseudo-Cushing's: alcohol excess or severe depression → mimics Cushing's biochemically (false-positive dexamethasone suppression test). Insulin stress test (or abstinence from alcohol) differentiates.
Clinical Features
Cortisol Excess (any cause)
  • Central obesity — truncal, with sparing of limbs; moon face; buffalo hump (cervical fat pad); supraclavicular fat pads
  • Purple striae — wide (>1cm), violaceous; abdomen, breasts, thighs — protein catabolism of skin; contrast with normal silvery narrow stretch marks
  • Thin, easily-bruised skin; poor wound healing
  • Proximal myopathy — difficulty rising from chair, climbing stairs
  • Osteoporosis — vertebral fractures; ↓ osteoblast activity

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Addison's Disease / Adren:
The Single Decisive Fork

The whole topic splits on where the HPA axis fails. Ask two questions: Is ACTH high or low? and Is aldosterone affected? — and every sign, electrolyte, and treatment deduces out.

Cortex anatomy anchor (G–F–R / salt–sugar–sex): Glomerulosa → aldosterone (RAAS) · Fasciculata → cortisol (ACTH) · Reticularis → androgens/DHEA. Explains which hormones fail in each type.
Primary (Addison's) — HIGH ACTH

Adrenal cortex destroyed → can't respond to ACTH → ACTH rises → melanocyte stimulation → bronze pigmentation. Both cortisol AND aldosterone fail → hyperkalaemia, salt craving, postural hypotension.

Secondary / Tertiary — LOW ACTH

Pituitary or hypothalamus fails → ACTH low → no pigmentation. Aldosterone is spared (RAAS is independent of ACTH) → no hyperkalaemia. Only cortisol deficient.

Primary (Addison's) = high ACTH + pigmented + hyperkalaemic + both hormones lost. Secondary = low ACTH + no pigmentation + aldosterone spared.

Short Synacthen Test

First-line. Failure of cortisol to rise to ≥550 nmol/L = adrenal insufficiency. ACTH level then localises (high = primary; low = secondary/tertiary).

Classic Biochemistry Quartet

Hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypotension + bronze pigmentation = primary Addison's. Hyperkalaemia only in primary (aldosterone loss).

Autoimmune Addison's

Commonest cause (developed world). 21-hydroxylase antibodies. Associated cluster: T1DM, thyroid disease, vitiligo, pernicious anaemia, coeliac.

Tertiary = Steroid Withdrawal

Paired Adrenal Tests

Synacthen (stimulation) = adrenal insufficiency. Dexamethasone (suppression) = Cushing's. Same axis, opposite question, opposite logic.

Sheehan's Syndrome

Post-partum pituitary necrosis → secondary adrenal insufficiency + hypothyroidism. Failure to lactate post-delivery is the classic clue.
ENDOCRINOLOGY__Phaeochromocytoma:
Overview & The Single Decisive Fork

Phaeochromocytoma = catecholamine-secreting tumour of chromaffin cells (adrenal medulla) → unregulated adrenaline released in bursts → paroxysmal symptoms.

Paraganglioma = the same tumour arising from extra-adrenal sympathetic ganglia (~15%).

The single decisive fork — α before β, always, no exceptions. Block alpha first (phenoxybenzamine), then add beta only once alpha is established. Getting it wrong is lethal: β-blockade first removes β-mediated vasodilation while leaving α-vasoconstriction unopposed → hypertensive crisis. Hold "unopposed alpha kills" and the whole management section deduces out.
Adrenal cluster cross-ref: Cortex = steroids (Cushing's / Addison's / Conn's). Medulla = catecholamines (this topic). Phaeochromocytoma completes the adrenal cluster.
The 10% Rule — Organising Scaffold
The 10% Rule
  • 10% malignant
  • 10% bilateral
  • 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma)
  • 10% familial
Genetic Associations (~40% hereditary)
  • MEN2 — medullary thyroid cancer + phaeochromocytoma ± parathyroid (MEN2A) / neuromas (MEN2B); RET oncogene
  • Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)
  • Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)

The 10% rule undersells hereditary phaeochromocytoma — truly ~40% genetic. Always offer genetic testing.

Pathophysiology

Chromaffin cells → catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline) → α and β adrenergic effects. The α/β split is the reason for the treatment sequence.

α-receptor effects
  • Vasoconstriction → ↑BP
  • ↑ peripheral resistance
  • ↑ glucose (glycogenolysis)
  • Pupil dilation
β-receptor effects
  • ↑HR (β₁)
  • ↑ contractility (β₁)
  • Vasodilation (β₂)
  • Bronchodilation (β₂)
Clinical Features
Classic triad (the SBA hook): Episodic headache + sweating + palpitations/tachycardia — on a background of hypertension. Classically paroxysmal. Can mimic a panic attack.

  • Palpitations / tachycardia
  • Anxiety / sense of doom
  • Tremor · pallor
  • Weight loss (↑BMR)
  • Postural hypotension (volume depletion)

Severe hypertension · hyperthermia · confusion · end-organ damage (cardiac/renal/neurological) → circulatory collapse.

Precipitated by: direct tumour manipulation, induction of anaesthesia, opioids, metoclopramide, contrast agents.

α Before β — Always

β-blockade first → unopposed α-vasoconstriction → hypertensive crisis. Phenoxybenzamine (α) first → propranolol (β) second. This is the lethal trap.

Episodic headache + sweating + palpitations + HTN = phaeochromocytoma until excluded. Paroxysmal. Can mimic panic attack.

Plasma free metanephrines (or 24h urinary metanephrines) — stable metabolites, elevated even between paroxysms. Not catecholamines.

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acromegaly:
Overview & The Two-Axis Spine

Acromegaly = excess growth hormone, almost always from a pituitary adenoma. GH acts indirectly via IGF-1 (liver) — which is why IGF-1, not GH, is the screening test.

The single decisive fork — a pituitary tumour does two separate things: (1) Mass effect (compresses optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia, compresses normal pituitary → hypopituitarism, headache) and (2) Hormone hypersecretion (GH → IGF-1 → tissue overgrowth). These two axes are independent. Hold "mass effect vs hormone effect" and the whole clinical picture and investigation logic deduces out.
Rare / special causes
  • Ectopic GHRH/GH — lung or pancreatic tumour (paraneoplastic)
  • Gigantism = same GH excess before epiphyseal fusion (children → linear height); acromegaly = after fusion (acral/soft-tissue growth) — same disease, timing-dependent
Pituitary cross-refs

The pituitary is the shared hub. A mass here can knock out other axes too → secondary hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency (Sheehan's), hypogonadism. ~⅓ of acromegaly tumours co-secrete prolactin (stalk effect or direct).

  • Bitemporal hemianopia — optic chiasm compression (classic sign)
  • Headache — dural stretch
  • Hypopituitarism — compression of normal pituitary → ↓ other hormones
  • Hyperprolactinaemia → galactorrhoea — stalk effect (~⅓ of cases)
GH / IGF-1 Excess (hormone effect)
  • Frontal bossing, prognathism, large nose
  • Macroglossia, interdental separation
  • Spade-like hands/feet — ↑ glove/ring/shoe size
  • Coarse sweaty/greasy skin
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome
  • Deep voice, jaw pain

Two-Axis Spine

Mass effect (bitemporal hemianopia, headache, hypopituitarism) + GH/IGF-1 excess (acral/soft-tissue growth). These are independent — a microadenoma can flood the body with GH without any mass effect.

IGF-1 = Screen; OGTT = Confirm

GH is pulsatile — do NOT measure directly. IGF-1 is stable. OGTT: failure to suppress GH = acromegaly. This is the gold-standard diagnostic test.

Bitemporal Hemianopia

Optic chiasm compression — the classic mass-effect sign. Order formal perimetry in all new pituitary masses.

Gigantism vs Acromegaly

Same GH excess. Pre-epiphyseal fusion (children) = gigantism (linear height). Post-fusion (adults) = acromegaly (acral/soft-tissue growth).

Surgery → Medical → Radiotherapy

Trans-sphenoidal surgery 1st-line. Then octreotide (somatostatin analogue), pegvisomant (GH-receptor antagonist), cabergoline (if prolactin co-secretion). Radiotherapy last resort.

GH is Diabetogenic

GH → insulin resistance → T2DM. Screen all patients. Also causes cardiomyopathy, HTN, OSA, arthropathy.

Colorectal Cancer Risk

GH/IGF-1 excess promotes colonic polyp growth. Surveillance colonoscopy is indicated in all patients with acromegaly.

Co-secretion & Hypopituitarism

~⅓ co-secrete prolactin → galactorrhoea. Mass can compress normal pituitary → screen all other axes (cortisol, TFTs, gonadotrophins).

Always give glucocorticoid first. Thyroxine first → increased metabolic demand → adrenal crisis. The "cover the adrenal axis" principle runs through myxoedema coma and hypopituitarism.

Sudden headache + visual loss + ophthalmoplegia. IV hydrocortisone first (adrenal crisis), then urgent MRI, then neurosurgical decompression.

Sheehan's = failed lactation post-PPH → panhypopituitarism. Kallmann's = isolated GnRH deficiency + anosmia (no smell + no puberty = Kallmann's).

In secondary hypothyroidism TSH is low/normal (not high). Monitor free T4, not TSH, to guide levothyroxine dosing.

Overview & The Dopamine-Brake Fork
The single decisive fork: prolactinoma (autonomous over-secretion) vs disinhibition (stalk compression, dopamine-blocking drugs, high TRH in hypothyroidism). The prolactin level resolves this: very high (>5000 mU/L) → prolactinoma; modest elevation → disinhibiting cause. Hold this and aetiology, investigation, and treatment all deduce.
Dopamine physiology anchor

Prolactin is under TONIC dopamine INHIBITION from the hypothalamus. Anything interrupting this → prolactin rises. This is why dopamine agonists (cabergoline) treat prolactinomas.

Completes the over-secretion trio

GH (acromegaly) · ACTH (Cushing's disease) · Prolactin (prolactinoma). Each anterior pituitary hormone can be over-secreted.

Autonomous Over-secretion

Benign prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma; commonest cause of true hyperprolactinaemia; level usually very high (>5000 mU/L). Microprolactinoma <10mm, macroprolactinoma >10mm.

Dopamine Brake Released (Disinhibition)
Stalk compression

Any pituitary/hypothalamic tumour compressing the pituitary stalk cuts dopamine delivery → modest prolactin rise. A non-secreting tumour can still raise prolactin this way (stalk effect).

Drugs (commonest overall in practice — always exclude first!)

Dopamine antagonists: metoclopramide, domperidone, antipsychotics/phenothiazines; also oestrogens, cimetidine, methyldopa.

Upstream Stimulation
Primary hypothyroidism

High TRH stimulates prolactin release (cross-ref hypothyroidism note).

Other

PCOS; acromegaly (~⅓ co-secrete prolactin + GH — cross-ref); pregnancy/physiological; renal failure (reduced clearance).

Prolactin → inhibits GnRH → hypogonadism — this mechanism explains the entire clinical picture: galactorrhoea (prolactin drives milk) + menstrual/fertility/libido effects (GnRH inhibition).

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of Inappropriate:
Overview & The Defining Paradox
SIADH = inappropriate ADH excess → water reabsorption in collecting ducts → dilutional (euvolaemic) hyponatraemia. ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insipidus:
Causes of Hypernatraemia (Na > 145 mmol/L)
Definition: Serum sodium >145 mmol/L. Always reflects a deficit of water relative to sodium. Hypernatraemia is a hyperosmolar state — water moves out of cells, causing cellular dehydration. The most common cause is inadequate water intake rather than excess sodium.
Category 1: Water Loss (Most Common)
Mechanism Examples Key Features
Insensible losses Fever, burns, sweating, tachypnoea Urine concentrated (Uosm >700); kidney conserving water appropriately
GI losses Diarrhoea, vomiting, fistulae — without adequate water replacement Often hypotonic fluid loss; urine concentrated
Diabetes Insipidus (cranial) ADH deficiency: trauma, pituitary surgery, tumour, sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis Polyuria, dilute urine (Uosm <300); responds to desmopressin
Diabetes Insipidus (nephrogenic) Lithium toxicity, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, inherited (AVPR2/AQP2 mutations), tubulointerstitial disease Dilute urine; does not respond to desmopressin; aquaporin-2 defect
Osmotic diuresis Hyperglycaemia (DKA/HHS), mannitol, urea, contrast agents Polyuria with isosthenuric/mildly concentrated urine; glucosuria in DKA
Loop diuretics Furosemide, bumetanide Hypotonic urine loss; commonly combined with poor oral intake in elderly
Category 2: Sodium Gain (Less Common)
Cause Examples Notes
Iatrogenic Hypertonic saline (3% NaCl), sodium bicarbonate infusion, TPN with insufficient free water Most common sodium-gain cause in hospital; review fluid prescriptions
Hyperaldosteronism Conn's syndrome, secondary hyperaldosteronism Sodium retention + hypokalaemia; hypertension; hypernatraemia often mild
Cushing's syndrome Excess cortisol (mineralocorticoid activity) Sodium and water retention; hypokalaemic alkalosis
Salt poisoning Child abuse, accidental ingestion, sea-water drowning Rare; urine sodium high; hypervolaemic hypernatraemia
Category 3: Impaired Thirst / Access to Water

Even with intact ADH, thirst is the primary defence against hypernatraemia. Impaired thirst leads to essential hypernatraemia (adipsia).

  • Hypothalamic damage: tumours (craniopharyngioma), surgery, sarcoidosis, trauma — destroys osmoreceptors
  • Elderly patients: blunted thirst perception; reduced renal concentrating ability; common in care homes
  • Intubated / obtunded patients: cannot self-regulate fluid intake; entirely dependent on prescribed fluids
  • Infants: dependent on carers; at risk with formula errors or diarrhoeal illness
Diagnostic Approach:
  1. Assess volume status (hypovolaemic / euvolaemic / hypervolaemic hypernatraemia)
  2. Urine osmolality + urine sodium:
    • Uosm >700 → appropriate renal response (extrarenal loss or inadequate intake)
    • Uosm <300 → diabetes insipidus
    • Uosm 300–700 → partial DI or osmotic diuresis
  3. Water deprivation test ± desmopressin to distinguish cranial vs nephrogenic DI
Management of Hypernatraemia
Critical Rule: Correct hypernatraemia SLOWLY. Brain cells adapt to hyperosmolality by accumulating idiogenic osmoles. Rapid correction → rapid cerebral swelling → cerebral oedema, seizures, herniation.

Maximum correction rate:
  • Chronic hypernatraemia (>48h or unknown duration): max 10–12 mmol/L/day (0.5 mmol/L/hr)
  • Acute hypernatraemia (<48h, known onset): can correct faster (1–2 mmol/L/hr)
Step Detail
1. Calculate Free Water Deficit (FWD) FWD (L) = TBW × (Nameasured / 140 − 1)
TBW = 0.6 × weight (men), 0.5 × weight (women/elderly)
e.g. 70 kg man, Na 160: TBW = 42 L; FWD = 42 × (160/140 − 1) = 6 L
2. Replace deficit over 48–72h Add ongoing losses + insensible losses (~500–1000 mL/day) to total replacement volume
3. Fluid choice
  • Oral water (preferred if patient can swallow)
  • IV 5% dextrose (free water; monitor glucose)
  • IV 0.45% NaCl (hypotonic saline — if also volume-depleted)
  • 0.9% NaCl if severely hypovolaemic (haemodynamic priority first)
4. Monitor Check serum Na every 4–6 hours; adjust infusion rate accordingly
5. Treat underlying cause Desmopressin for cranial DI; discontinue lithium/offending drug for nephrogenic DI; treat hyperglycaemia; review sodium-containing infusions
Treatment Summary by Cause:
  • Cranial DI: Intranasal/oral desmopressin (DDAVP) + free water
  • Nephrogenic DI: Low-sodium diet, thiazide diuretics (paradoxically reduce urine output), NSAIDs (indomethacin), amiloride (for lithium-induced)
  • Osmotic diuresis: Treat hyperglycaemia; stop mannitol; ensure free water replacement
  • Iatrogenic: Stop hypertonic fluids; replace free water deficit
Overview & The Decisive Fork
The single decisive fork: cranial (no ADH made) vs nephrogenic (kidney can't respond to ADH). The diagnostic resolver: does giving desmopressin fix it? Cranial = hypothalamus/pituitary fails to produce ADH → kidney is fine and responds to desmopressin (urine concentrates). Nephrogenic = ADH present but kidney can't respond → desmopressin does nothing (urine stays dilute). Hold 'can desmopressin rescue it?' and the whole topic deduces out.
ADH physiology anchor

ADH made in hypothalamus, secreted by posterior pituitary, acts on collecting ducts to reabsorb water. DI = inability to concentrate urine → polyuria + polydipsia + dilute urine despite high/normal serum osmolality.

Mirror — cross-ref SIADH

SIADH = too much ADH → concentrated urine + hyponatraemia. DI = too little/no response → dilute urine + hypernatraemia. Build them as the water-balance pair. Also: 'diabetes' here = Greek 'to pass through' (polyuria) — nothing to do with glucose; DI has normal blood sugar.

Surgical (Commonest)

Autoimmune

  • Radiation damage

Hypocalcaemia affects excitable membranes — neuromuscular irritability is the hallmark.

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Balance:
Overview — The Two Controllers
The single decisive fork: pH tells you the disturbance; CO₂ vs HCO₃⁻ tells you the system. pH → acidosis (<7.35) or alkalosis (>7.45). CO₂ is the respiratory/lung control (fast, minutes). HCO₃⁻ is the metabolic/kidney control (slow, hours–days). Match the abnormal one to the pH direction and you have the primary disturbance. That is it.
The Core Relationship

Henderson-Hasselbalch in words: pH ∝ HCO₃⁻ / CO₂ — bicarbonate on top (base), CO₂ on the bottom (acid).

  • ↑CO₂ → more acid → pH ↓
  • ↓HCO₃⁻ → less base → pH ↓
  • ↓CO₂ → less acid → pH ↑
  • ↑HCO₃⁻ → more base → pH ↑
Normal Values to Anchor
  • pH 7.35–7.45
  • CO₂ (PaCO₂) 4.7–6.0 kPa
  • HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mmol/L
  • Base excess (BE) ±2
  • PaO₂ 11–13 kPa (on air)
The Four Primary Disturbances
Reading rule: Respiratory disturbances → pH and CO₂ move in OPPOSITE directions. Metabolic disturbances → pH and HCO₃⁻ move in the SAME direction. This single line decodes the entire grid.
DisturbancepHPrimary problemCompensation
Respiratory acidosis↓CO₂ ↑ (hypoventilation)Kidneys retain HCO₃⁻ (days)
Respiratory alkalosis↑CO₂ ↓ (hyperventilation)Kidneys excrete HCO₃⁻ (days)
Metabolic acidosis↓HCO₃⁻ ↓ (acid added or base lost)Lungs blow off CO₂ — Kussmaul (minutes)
Metabolic alkalosis↑HCO₃⁻ ↑ (base gained or H⁺ lost)Lungs hypoventilate, retain CO₂ (limited)
The 5-Step ABG Algorithm
Run every ABG through these five questions in order. Compensation never fully overshoots — if pH has crossed to the opposite side, suspect a mixed (second primary) disturbance.
Step 1Oxygenation — PaO₂ / SpO₂. Is there hypoxia or type 1/type 2 respiratory failure? (Separate question from the acid-base analysis.)
Step 2pH — acidosis (<7.35) or alkalosis (>7.45)? If mid-range, consider a compensated or mixed picture.
Step 3CO₂ — does it explain the pH? ↑CO₂ with ↓pH = respiratory acidosis. ↓CO₂ with ↑pH = respiratory alkalosis.
Step 4HCO₃⁻ — does it explain the pH? ↓HCO₃⁻ with ↓pH = metabolic acidosis. ↑HCO₃⁻ with ↑pH = metabolic alkalosis.
Step 5Compensation — is the other system correcting? Partial (pH still abnormal) vs full (pH back in range). If pH has crossed the opposite direction → mixed disturbance.
Respiratory Acid-Base
Respiratory Acidosis — ↑CO₂

Mechanism: hypoventilation — cannot clear CO₂

  • COPD / type 2 respiratory failure — commonest; chronic high HCO₃⁻ is the renal compensation clue
  • Opioids / sedation / anaesthesia
  • Neuromuscular disease (GBS, MG, motor neurone disease)
  • Chest wall deformity, obesity hypoventilation
  • Severe asthma — late/exhausted (CO₂ rising = danger sign)
Respiratory Alkalosis — ↓CO₂

Mechanism: hyperventilation — blowing off CO₂

  • Anxiety / panic attack — commonest; perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm
  • Pain
  • PE — hypoxia drives hyperventilation
  • High altitude
  • Sepsis (early) — direct respiratory centre stimulation
  • Salicylates (early) — direct resp centre stimulation before metabolic acidosis develops
COPD cross-ref: chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation — chronically elevated HCO₃⁻ (often 30+) is normal for them. During exacerbation, CO₂ rises further. A "normal" pH in a COPD patient may mask a worsening acidosis.
Metabolic Acidosis — Split by Anion Gap
The anion gap [= Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), normal 8–14 mmol/L] is the key sub-fork. It separates added acid (gap raised — unmeasured anions present) from lost bicarbonate (gap normal — Cl⁻ replaces HCO₃⁻, hyperchloraemic acidosis).
Raised Anion Gap — Added Acid

MUDPILES mnemonic:

  • Methanol poisoning
  • Uraemia (renal failure)
  • DKA — ketoacids (cross-ref DKA)
  • Propylene glycol
  • Isoniazid / Iron overdose
  • Lactate — lactic acidosis (sepsis, shock, ischaemia, metformin)
  • Ethylene glycol (antifreeze)
  • Salicylates (late metabolic component)
Normal Anion Gap — Lost HCO₃⁻

Chloride rises to replace lost bicarbonate (hyperchloraemic acidosis):

  • GI bicarbonate loss — diarrhoea (commonest)
  • Renal tubular acidosis (RTA types 1, 2, 4)
  • Addison's disease
  • Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor)
  • Saline excess (dilutional)
  • Ureteric diversion (ileal conduit)
Compensation = Kussmaul respiration — deep, rapid breathing blowing off CO₂ to correct pH. Classic in DKA. If CO₂ is NOT low in metabolic acidosis, the patient is failing to compensate — respiratory fatigue or mixed disturbance.
Metabolic Alkalosis
Compensation for metabolic alkalosis is limited — hypoventilation to retain CO₂ is constrained by the hypoxic drive. pH rarely fully corrects.
Causes — Loss of H⁺ or Gain of Base
  • Vomiting — loss of gastric H⁺ (HCl); the classic cause
  • NG suction
  • Loop/thiazide diuretics — H⁺ and K⁺ loss in urine
  • Conn's syndrome / hyperaldosteronism — aldosterone drives H⁺ and K⁺ excretion in exchange for Na⁺ reabsorption (cross-ref)
  • Hypokalaemia (intracellular H⁺ shift)
  • Antacid or alkali excess
  • Milk-alkali syndrome
Biochemical Pattern
  • pH ↑, HCO₃⁻ ↑ (primary)
  • CO₂ ↑ (compensation — hypoventilation)
  • K⁺ often LOW (co-lost with H⁺)
  • Cl⁻ often LOW (co-lost in vomiting)
  • Urine Cl⁻ <20 = saline-responsive (vomiting, diuretics); >20 = saline-resistant (Conn's, Bartter's)
Pattern Recognition — Classic ABG Vignettes
Learn these six patterns cold. Each maps a clinical scenario to its ABG signature in seconds.

COPD exacerbation, drowsy↓↑↑↑ (chronic comp)Respiratory acidosis, partly compensated
Panic attack, tingling hands↑↓NormalRespiratory alkalosis (acute)
DKA, Kussmaul breathing↓↓ (comp)↓↓Raised-gap metabolic acidosis
Profuse vomiting↑↑ (comp)↑↑Metabolic alkalosis
Severe diarrhoea↓↓ (comp)↓↓Normal-gap metabolic acidosis
Aspirin overdoseVariable↓↓MIXED: resp alkalosis + raised-gap metabolic acidosis
Salicylate (aspirin) overdose — the favourite SBA trap: Early = direct respiratory centre stimulation → respiratory alkalosis (↓CO₂, ↑pH). Late = salicylate metabolism → raised-gap metabolic acidosis (↓HCO₃⁻, ↓pH). ABG shows MIXED picture — respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis simultaneously. The CO₂ is low and the HCO₃⁻ is low, but the pH depends on which is dominant.
Exam Pearls
pH = direction; CO₂ vs HCO₃⁻ = which system. The whole topic in one sentence.
Respiratory: pH and CO₂ move OPPOSITE. Metabolic: pH and HCO₃⁻ move SAME direction.
CO₂ = lungs (fast, minutes). HCO₃⁻ = kidneys (slow, days). Respiratory compensation is quick; metabolic (renal) takes 3–5 days.
Compensation never overshoots. If pH crossed the other side, it is a mixed disturbance — two primary problems.
Metabolic acidosis → always calculate the anion gap → MUDPILES (raised) vs GI/renal loss (normal).
Kussmaul breathing = respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis. Seen in DKA. If CO₂ not falling in met acidosis → respiratory fatigue.
Salicylate OD = mixed (early resp alkalosis + late raised-gap metabolic acidosis). Vomiting = metabolic alkalosis. COPD = chronic resp acidosis with high HCO₃⁻.
COPD chronic adaption: do not be reassured by a normal pH in a COPD patient if HCO₃⁻ is chronically high — the true acidosis may be masked.
ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndrome / Endocri:
Overview — The Renin Fork
Hyperaldosteronism = excess aldosterone → hypertension + hypokalaemia. KEY TRAP: K⁺ is normal in 60–90% of cases — do NOT exclude on normal potassium. Conn's syndrome = adrenal adenoma (one cause among several — bilateral hyperplasia is commoner). The fork: primary (adrenal autonomous, low renin) vs secondary (RAAS-driven, high renin).
Why It Matters

Common under-diagnosed cause of secondary / resistant hypertension. Cross-ref adrenal cluster: Cushing's (cortisol excess), Addison's (adrenal deficiency — the mirror), phaeochromocytoma (catecholamines).

The Classic Picture

HTN + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis. BUT K⁺ is normal in the majority — don't rely on it.

Aldosterone's 3 actions explain everything: ↑Na⁺ reabsorption → ↑BP; ↑K⁺ secretion → hypokalaemia; ↑H⁺ secretion → metabolic alkalosis. Cross-ref Acid-Base Balance.

RAAS Physiology Anchor
Hold this chain and the whole topic deduces out: Low BP → Renin (juxtaglomerular cells) → Angiotensin I (liver) → ACE (lungs) → Angiotensin II → Aldosterone (adrenal cortex zona glomerulosa) → acts on distal nephron.
Aldosterone ActionResultClinical Consequence
↑Na⁺ reabsorption↑Water retentionHypertension (volume expansion)
↑K⁺ secretion↓K⁺Hypokalaemia, muscle weakness, polyuria
↑H⁺ secretion↓H⁺Metabolic alkalosis
Aetiology — Primary vs Secondary
Aldosterone is HIGH in both. Renin separates them: LOW renin = adrenal autonomy (primary); HIGH renin = kidney/RAAS driving it (secondary).

PrimaryBilateral adrenal hyperplasia (commonest)LOWAdrenal autonomy — independent of renin

Clinical Features
Hypertension

Volume expansion from Na⁺ retention. Usually asymptomatic. Often diagnosed incidentally or when investigating resistant HTN. Long-standing → CKD, stroke, HF, retinopathy.

Hypokalaemia Features (minority)

Muscle weakness, fatigue, cramps. Paraesthesia. Polyuria / nocturia (nephrogenic DI mechanism — high K⁺ flux impairs concentrating ability). Mood disturbance.

REMEMBER: K⁺ normal in 60–90% — absence of hypokalaemia does NOT rule out.

When to Screen
  • Resistant HTN (≥3 antihypertensives at adequate dose)
  • HTN + spontaneous hypokalaemia (K⁺ <3.5 without diuretics)
  • HTN + diuretic-induced severe hypokalaemia
  • HTN in young patient (<40)
  • Adrenal incidentaloma + HTN
Investigations
Step 1 — Screen: Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR)ARR = aldosterone ÷ renin. ↑Aldosterone + ↓renin → raised ARR → PRIMARY. ↑Aldosterone + ↑renin → SECONDARY. Stop interfering drugs first: spironolactone (4 weeks), ACEi/ARBs, β-blockers (2 weeks) — all distort results.
↓
Step 2 — Confirm: Saline Suppression TestIV saline infusion — aldosterone fails to suppress in primary hyperaldosteronism (autonomous secretion). Confirms diagnosis if ARR raised.
↓
Step 3 — Localise: CT/MRI → Adrenal Vein SamplingCT/MRI adrenals: identify adenoma vs hyperplasia (imaging alone insufficient — small adenomas missed). Adrenal vein sampling (AVS): gold standard to distinguish unilateral adenoma (→ surgery) from bilateral hyperplasia (→ medical).
CRITICAL: Do NOT skip adrenal vein sampling to go straight to surgery based on CT alone. CT misses ~30% of small adenomas and may incorrectly lateralise.
Management
The decision node: UNILATERAL adenoma → surgery (curative). BILATERAL hyperplasia → medical (lifelong MR antagonist). This fork is the entire management question.
Unilateral Adenoma (Conn's)

Laparoscopic adrenalectomy — curative in most.

Pre-op: correct hypokalaemia; spironolactone while awaiting surgery. Post-op: BP often improves significantly; may resolve entirely.

Bilateral Hyperplasia

Spironolactone (first-line MR antagonist). Side effects: gynaecomastia, erectile dysfunction, menstrual irregularity.

Eplerenone — more selective, fewer anti-androgen effects; preferred if side effects problematic.

Secondary Hyperaldosteronism

Treat the underlying cause: renal artery stenosis (angioplasty ± stent); heart failure / cirrhosis (treat primary condition). ACEi/ARB address the RAAS axis.

Exam Pearls
The fork: aldosterone HIGH in both. Renin discriminates — LOW renin = primary (adrenal autonomy); HIGH renin = secondary (kidney driving it).
K⁺ trap: normal potassium in 60–90% of primary hyperaldosteronism. Do NOT exclude on normal K⁺.
Conn's = adrenal adenoma — but bilateral hyperplasia is the COMMONEST cause of primary hyperaldosteronism overall.
ARR = screening test. Stop interfering drugs before: spironolactone (4 weeks), ACEi/ARBs, β-blockers (2 weeks).
Adrenal vein sampling = gold standard to lateralise. CT alone misses ~30% of adenomas and can mis-lateralise — never skip AVS.
Decision: unilateral adenoma → laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone / eplerenone.
Addison's mirror: aldosterone deficiency → low Na⁺, high K⁺, metabolic acidosis — exact opposite of hyperaldosteronism.
Metabolic alkalosis + hypokalaemia on any ABG → think hyperaldosteronism. Cross-ref Acid-Base Balance.
ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyroidism / Hyp:
Overview — The PTH Fork
The single decisive fork: Is PTH high or suppressed? A normal parathyroid gland responds to high calcium by switching PTH off. If it hasn't switched off, the gland is the problem. If it has, hunt for the non-PTH cause — almost always malignancy.
PTHCalciumCause
High / inappropriately normalHighPrimary HPT (adenoma), tertiary HPT, FHH
Suppressed (low)HighMalignancy (PTHrP, bone mets, myeloma), vit D excess, sarcoid, thiazides
The 90% Rule

Primary hyperparathyroidism + malignancy = 90% of all hypercalcaemia. Outpatient = usually adenoma. Inpatient = usually malignancy.

PTH Physiology Anchor

PTH ↑Ca and ↓phosphate — bone resorption, renal Ca reabsorption + phosphate excretion, activates vit D. Therefore primary HPT → ↑Ca + low phosphate.

Causes of Hypercalcaemia
PTH-Driven — Gland is the Problem
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism — parathyroid adenoma (commonest); commonest outpatient cause of hypercalcaemia
  • Tertiary hyperparathyroidism — autonomous hyperplasia after long-standing secondary HPT (classic: post-renal transplant)
  • Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) — Ca-sensing receptor mutation; ↑Ca + ↑PTH but LOW urinary Ca; benign mimic — do NOT operate
Non-PTH — PTH is Correctly Suppressed
  • Malignancy (commonest inpatient cause):
    • PTHrP — squamous cell carcinoma, SCLC; mimics PTH but PTH itself is suppressed
    • Bone metastases — direct osteolysis (breast, lung, prostate)
    • Myeloma — osteoclast-activating cytokines
  • Vitamin D excess — supplementation overdose
  • Sarcoidosis — granulomas activate vit D autonomously
  • Thiazide diuretics, milk-alkali syndrome, immobilisation
The Three Types of Hyperparathyroidism
TypeCausePTHCalcium

The logic chain: Secondary HPT is an appropriate PTH response to low calcium (not a gland disease). After years of this stimulus, glands become autonomous — they keep secreting PTH even after the cause is fixed (e.g. post-renal transplant). This is tertiary HPT. Cross-ref CKD for the classic secondary→tertiary pathway.
Clinical Features — "Stones, Bones, Groans, Moans"

  • Renal calculi (Ca²⁺ stones)
  • Polyuria / nocturia (nephrogenic DI effect — cross-ref DI note)
  • Chronic kidney disease

  • Bone pain, osteoporosis, fractures
  • Osteitis fibrosa cystica (severe/chronic)
  • X-ray: pepperpot skull, subperiosteal resorption

  • Constipation, nausea, vomiting
  • Pancreatitis, peptic ulcers
  • Fatigue, depression, confusion, psychosis ("psychic overtones")
The mirror pearl: Hypercalcaemia = sluggish membranes → short QT. Hypocalcaemia = excitable membranes → long QT. They are the cardiac ECG pair.
Investigations
Calcium + Phosphate + PTH
Core triad. Primary HPT: ↑Ca, ↓phosphate, ↑PTH. PTH suppressed → hunt malignancy
24h Urinary Calcium
Exclude FHH (↑Ca + ↑PTH but LOW urinary Ca). Must not operate on FHH — always check before surgery

If PTH suppressed: PTHrP (SCLC/squamous), protein electrophoresis (myeloma), imaging for bone mets
Localisation (surgery planned)

X-Ray (severe/chronic)

Acute Severe Hypercalcaemia (Emergency)
Sequence matters — IV saline FIRST, then bisphosphonate. Never bisphosphonate before rehydration. Never give dextrose.
Step 1 — IV Saline Rehydration0.9% NaCl 4–6 L/24h. These patients are profoundly dehydrated from calcium-driven polyuria. Rehydration is the single most important step.
↓

↓
Step 3 — Adjuncts if neededCalcitonin (faster but transient). Steroids if myeloma, sarcoidosis, or vit D excess (block gut absorption and vit D activation).
Primary Hyperparathyroidism
Parathyroidectomy (Definitive)

Surgical removal of the adenoma. Indicated if: Ca >0.25 mmol/L above upper limit, age <50, or end-organ damage (stones, osteoporosis, CKD, symptoms).

Conservative / Medical

If all three: Ca <0.25 above limit and age >50 and no end-organ damage. Cinacalcet (calcimimetic — activates Ca-sensing receptor → ↓PTH) if unfit for or declines surgery.

Secondary & Tertiary
  • Secondary HPT — treat the underlying cause (vit D replacement, CKD management)
  • Tertiary HPT — subtotal parathyroidectomy (remove the autonomous hyperplastic tissue)

The fork: High Ca + HIGH PTH = parathyroid (primary/tertiary/FHH). High Ca + SUPPRESSED PTH = malignancy.

Malignancy: Commonest inpatient cause. PTHrP (SCLC/squamous), bone mets, myeloma — PTH is suppressed in all.

Secondary → tertiary: Secondary HPT is appropriate (Ca low/normal). Tertiary = autonomous after chronic secondary. Classic: post-renal transplant with persisting high Ca.

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ovary Syndrome:
Overview & Mechanism Spine
The single mechanism spine: Insulin resistance → ↑insulin → ↑LH → ↑androgen production by ovarian theca cells → anovulation + hyperandrogenism. This one chain explains PCOS, its metabolic complications, and its treatments.
The Hormonal Axis
  • ↑LH:FSH ratio [typically >2:1] — LH dominates → drives androgen production
  • ↑Insulin suppresses SHBG [sex hormone binding globulin] → more free androgen circulates
  • ↑Androgen → anovulation → oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea + polycystic ovaries
The Metabolic Axis
  • Insulin resistance → hyperinsulinaemia → type 2 DM risk
  • Obesity worsens insulin resistance [present in ~50–80%]
  • Dyslipidaemia [↑triglycerides, ↓HDL]
  • ↑Cardiovascular risk long-term
  • Endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed oestrogen [anovulation means no progesterone phase]
Rotterdam Criteria — Diagnosis Requires 2 of 3
Rotterdam criteria: diagnosis requires 2 of 3 features. Other causes of hyperandrogenism (CAH, Cushing's, androgen-secreting tumour, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease) must be excluded first.
1. Oligo/Anovulation
  • Irregular periods [oligomenorrhoea <9/year or amenorrhoea]
  • Anovulatory cycles → infertility
2. Clinical/Biochemical Hyperandrogenism
  • Clinical: hirsutism [Ferriman-Gallwey score], acne, male-pattern alopecia
  • Biochemical: raised total/free testosterone, raised DHEAS
3. Polycystic Ovaries on Ultrasound
  • ≥12 follicles 2–9mm in one ovary OR ovarian volume >10 mL
  • Note: polycystic morphology alone is NOT diagnostic — 20–30% of normal women have it

Exclude differential causes before diagnosing PCOS: 17-OHP (CAH), 24h urinary cortisol or dexamethasone suppression (Cushing's), prolactin (hyperprolactinaemia), TFTs (thyroid). Androgen-secreting tumour — suspect if testosterone very high (>5 nmol/L) or virilisation.
Clinical Features
Reproductive Features
  • Oligomenorrhoea / amenorrhoea [irregular or absent periods]
  • Anovulatory infertility [cannot conceive naturally without ovulation]
  • Recurrent miscarriage
  • Endometrial hyperplasia / carcinoma risk [unopposed oestrogen from anovulation]
Hyperandrogenic Features
  • Hirsutism [excess terminal hair in male distribution — face, chest, abdomen, thighs]
  • Acne [androgen-driven sebum production]
  • Male-pattern alopecia [frontal/vertex hair thinning]
  • Clitoromegaly [if severe]
Metabolic Features
  • Obesity [central adiposity, BMI often elevated]
  • Acanthosis nigricans [velvety hyperpigmented skin at neck/axillae — insulin resistance marker]

Management — By Problem (The Critical Conflict)
CRITICAL CONFLICT: COCP treats cycles and hirsutism. Clomifene (or letrozole) is needed for fertility. You CANNOT use COCP if trying to conceive — these are mutually exclusive treatments. This conflict is the exam question.
Step 1All patients: Lifestyle — weight loss improves all features (insulin resistance, periods, androgens, fertility). Even 5–10% weight loss restores ovulation in many. First-line before drugs.
Step 2Irregular cycles + hirsutism/acne (NOT trying to conceive): COCP [combined oral contraceptive pill]. Regulates cycles [withdrawal bleeds], reduces androgen [oestrogen ↑SHBG, reduces free androgen]. Best: Dianette [co-cyprindiol — contains anti-androgen cyproterone acetate] for hirsutism/acne. Step 3Fertility (trying to conceive): Clomifene [anti-oestrogen — stimulates FSH → ovulation induction]. Now 2nd line — letrozole [aromatase inhibitor] preferred in many centres (better live birth rates, fewer multiple pregnancies). Metformin: insulin sensitiser; improves cycle regularity + may restore ovulation; adjunct to clomifene in insulin-resistant PCOS.
Step 4Refractory / adjuncts: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling [surgical — ovarian diathermy restores ovulation in clomifene-resistant cases]. Eflornithine cream [topical — slows facial hair growth, not a systemic treatment]. Spironolactone [anti-androgen — used off-label for hirsutism, contraindicated in pregnancy].
Metformin: reduces insulin resistance → lowers androgen → may restore ovulation. Can be used long-term for metabolic risk reduction. Does not directly treat hirsutism.

LH:FSH ratio >2:1 supports PCOS but is NOT a diagnostic criterion — Rotterdam is the standard.
Endometrial cancer risk from unopposed oestrogen (anovulation → no progesterone luteal phase). Induce withdrawal bleeds if amenorrhoeic for >3 months.
Letrozole now preferred over clomifene for ovulation induction in many centres — better live birth rates, lower multiple pregnancy risk.

No insulin → ↑glycogenolysis / gluconeogenesis, ↓glucose uptake, ↑lipolysis → ketones. This chain ends in DKA — raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (cross-ref DKA note).

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabetes:
Overview — Resistance + Relative Deficiency
T2DM = peripheral insulin resistance + inadequate insulin secretion → chronic hyperglycaemia. The fork: T2 = relative deficiency + resistance (insidious, HHS-prone, stepwise treatment) vs T1 = absolute autoimmune deficiency.
Pathophysiology chain

Chronic glucose/insulin exposure → cells resist insulin → β-cells compensate, then fatigue → less insulin → chronic hyperglycaemia → micro/macrovascular complications.

Insulin physiology anchor: Insulin stores nutrients (glycogenesis, ↓gluconeogenesis, ↓lipolysis, GLUT4 translocation). Opposed by counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, GH).

Risk Factors
Non-modifiable
  • Older age
  • Ethnicity — South Asian, Black, Chinese (higher prevalence at lower BMI)
  • Family history (stronger genetic link than T1 — twin concordance ~50–90%)
Modifiable
  • Obesity — central adiposity drives insulin resistance
  • Sedentary lifestyle
  • Metabolic syndrome cluster — cross-ref HTN, dyslipidaemia, PCOS (insulin resistance threads through all)
Clinical Features
Osmotic / Metabolic
  • Often risk-factor profile is the prompt; symptoms milder/slower than T1
  • Fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, glycosuria
  • Acanthosis nigricans — velvety hyperpigmentation of skin folds; hallmark of insulin resistance
Infections (glucose feeds pathogens)
  • Candida — oral thrush, balanitis, pruritus vulvae
  • Slow-healing wounds, recurrent UTIs
  • Younger patients can present acutely (even DKA); older patients insidiously

Metabolic Syndrome — Definition & Diagnostic Criteria

Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of cardiometabolic risk factors that occur together, significantly amplifying cardiovascular and type 2 diabetes risk. Two major frameworks are in common use:

IDF Consensus Criteria (2006) — requires central obesity PLUS ≥2 of the following:
  • Central obesity (mandatory): waist circumference ≥94 cm (M) or ≥80 cm (F) — Europid; ≥90 cm (M) or ≥80 cm (F) — South Asian / Chinese / Japanese
  • Triglycerides ≥1.7 mmol/L (or on TG-lowering treatment)
  • HDL-cholesterol <1.03 mmol/L (M) or <1.29 mmol/L (F) (or on HDL-raising treatment)
  • Blood pressure ≥130/85 mmHg (or on antihypertensive treatment)
  • Fasting plasma glucose ≥5.6 mmol/L (or previously diagnosed T2DM)

Pathophysiology

The central driver is insulin resistance, closely linked to excess visceral adipose tissue:

  1. Visceral fat releases free fatty acids (FFAs), adipokines (↓adiponectin, ↑TNF-α, ↑IL-6, ↑resistin) → hepatic and peripheral insulin resistance.
  2. Compensatory hyperinsulinaemia → promotes sodium retention (↑BP), stimulates hepatic VLDL synthesis (↑TG, ↓HDL), drives sympathetic overactivity.
  3. Pro-inflammatory state: ↑CRP, ↑fibrinogen, ↑PAI-1 → endothelial dysfunction → accelerated atherosclerosis.
  4. Hyperglycaemia develops when pancreatic β-cell compensation fails.
Key numbers: Metabolic syndrome confers a 5× increased risk of T2DM and a 2× increased cardiovascular risk compared with the general population.

Lifestyle modification is first-line and can reverse metabolic syndrome:
  • Weight loss 5–10% of body weight improves all components
  • Mediterranean or low-glycaemic-index diet
  • Physical activity ≥150 min/week moderate intensity
  • Smoking cessation (smoking worsens insulin resistance)

Secondary Causes of Diabetes — Overview

Secondary diabetes arises from an identifiable underlying cause other than primary autoimmune (T1DM) or polygenic insulin resistance (T2DM). It accounts for approximately 1–5% of all diabetes cases. Recognising the cause is essential as treatment of the underlying condition may improve or resolve hyperglycaemia.

Key diagnostic tool — C-peptide:
  • Low/absent C-peptide: absolute insulin deficiency — T1DM, total pancreatectomy, advanced chronic pancreatitis
  • Normal/high C-peptide: insulin resistance or excess insulin secretion — T2DM, Cushing's, acromegaly, drug-induced
  • Detectable C-peptide + young age + family history: consider MODY (helps distinguish from T1DM where C-peptide is undetectable)

ENDOCRINOLOGY__DKA:
Overview — The Biochemical Triad
DKA = life-threatening emergency. Biochemical triad: hyperglycaemia + ketonaemia + acidosis. This is the "no insulin → ketones" decompensation from the T1DM note. T2DM retains enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis → HHS instead. Cross-ref Acid-Base Balance (DKA = the textbook raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis).
Precipitants — "The I's"
  • Infection — commonest precipitant (sepsis drives counter-regulatory hormones)
  • Insulin omission / interruption — missed doses, pump failure
  • Intercurrent illness — MI, surgery, trauma
  • Initial presentation — first presentation of undiagnosed T1DM
Pathogenesis — Two Parallel Arms
Arm 1 — Glucose

No insulin → ↑gluconeogenesis / ↑glycogenolysis → hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → profound dehydration + electrolyte loss

Arm 2 — Ketones

No insulin → ↑lipolysis → free fatty acids → hepatic ketogenesis → acidic ketones → metabolic acidosis → vomiting → worsens dehydration

Both arms are accelerated by stress hormones (catecholamines, glucagon, cortisol). Vomiting from ketoacidosis worsens dehydration — a vicious cycle that kills if untreated.
Clinical Features
Dehydration (often 5–8L)
  • Sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, dry tongue
  • Hypotension, tachycardia, shock
  • Polyuria / polydipsia (osmotic diuresis)
GI / Respiratory
  • Vomiting, abdominal pain (can mimic surgical abdomen)
  • Kussmaul respiration — deep, rapid; blowing off CO₂ to compensate acidosis
  • Acetone breath (pear-drop smell)
Neurological
  • Lethargy, confusion
  • Impaired consciousness / coma in severe cases
  • Headache (early sign of cerebral oedema — a red flag)
Investigations — JBDS Diagnostic Criteria
Hyperglycaemia

Glucose >11 mmol/L (or known diabetic at any glucose if ketonaemia + acidosis present)

Ketonaemia

Blood ketones >3 mmol/L (finger-prick) or 2+ on urine dipstick

Acidosis

pH <7.3 and/or HCO₃⁻ <15 mmol/L — raised anion gap (ketones are the unmeasured anions)

The potassium paradox — the single most important investigation point:
Total body K⁺ is LOW (osmotic diuresis depletes it) but serum K⁺ is HIGH/normal on admission — because absent insulin lets K⁺ shift OUT of cells. Insulin treatment then drives K⁺ back in → serum K⁺ crashes → fatal arrhythmia if not pre-empted. This is why you check K⁺ before every step.
Other Investigations
  • U&E — urea/creatinine raised (dehydration); K⁺ as above
  • FBC, CRP, blood cultures — septic screen (infection is the commonest precipitant)
  • ECG — hyperkalaemia on admission; later hypokalaemia with treatment
  • Septic screen: MSU, CXR, wound swabs
Management — Fluids, Insulin, Potassium
The mantra: fluids first, then insulin, watch potassium. Two iatrogenic killers: (1) hypokalaemia from insulin driving K⁺ into cells; (2) cerebral oedema from over-rapid correction.
Step 1 — IV Fluids (0.9% Saline) — FIRSTAggressive rehydration — often 5–8L deficit. Start even if acidotic. Restores perfusion. Fluids before insulin — do NOT start insulin first.
↓
Step 2 — Fixed-Rate IV Insulin Infusion (0.1 units/kg/hr)Switches off ketogenesis. Continue long-acting background insulin; stop short-acting. Add 10% dextrose once glucose <14 mmol/L — keep insulin running to clear ketones (do NOT stop insulin to protect glucose).
↓
Step 3 — Potassium Replacement (per serum level)K⁺ >5.5 → none. K⁺ 3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L in fluids. K⁺ <3.5 → senior review; do NOT start insulin until K⁺ replaced (insulin will crash it further → fatal arrhythmia).
Iatrogenic Killer 1 — Hypokalaemia

Insulin drives K⁺ into cells → serum K⁺ crashes → fatal arrhythmia. Pre-empt: check K⁺ before starting insulin; replace if <3.5; reassess every 1–2h.

Iatrogenic Killer 2 — Cerebral Oedema

From over-rapid correction of glucose/osmolality. Headache + irritability + ↓GCS. Higher risk in young/children. Correct glucose slowly. Same principle as osmotic demyelination in SIADH.

Resolution Targets & Transition
  • Ketones <0.6 mmol/L, pH >7.3, HCO₃⁻ >15 = resolved
  • Transition to subcutaneous insulin — overlap with IV infusion by 30–60 min before stopping
  • Bicarbonate NOT routine — only pH <7.0 under senior guidance; risks paradoxical intracellular acidosis
Exam Pearls
The triad: glucose >11 + ketones >3 + pH <7.3 / HCO₃⁻ <15. Raised anion gap. DKA = T1 emergency.
Precipitants — the I's: Infection (commonest), Insulin omission, Intercurrent illness, Initial T1 presentation.
Kussmaul breathing = respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis. If CO₂ is NOT falling → respiratory fatigue / mixed disturbance. Cross-ref Acid-Base.
Potassium paradox: serum K⁺ high on admission (cells shift), total body K⁺ low. Insulin crashes serum K⁺ → fatal arrhythmia. Replace K⁺ before/during insulin.
Don't start insulin if K⁺ <3.5 — replace first. K⁺ 3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L in fluids. K⁺ >5.5 → none.
Add dextrose when glucose <14 — but keep insulin running to clear ketones. Do NOT stop insulin to protect glucose.
Cerebral oedema from over-rapid correction — young patients most at risk. Headache + ↓GCS = red flag. Correct slowly.
Bicarbonate NOT routine. Continue long-acting insulin; stop short-acting during infusion.
ENDOCRINOLOGY__HHS:
Overview — The T2 Metabolic Emergency
HHS = marked hyperglycaemia + hyperosmolality + mild/no ketosis. The metabolic emergency of uncontrolled T2DM — often elderly, often previously undiagnosed. Residual insulin blocks ketogenesis. The two dangers: extreme osmolality → altered consciousness and hyperviscosity → thrombosis.
Pathophysiology Chain

Relative insulin lack + ↑counter-regulatory hormones → profound hyperglycaemia → ↑osmolality → massive osmotic diuresis → severe volume depletion. But residual insulin blocks ketogenesis → no acidosis, no ketones.

Three SBA discriminators: Ketones/acidosis present = DKA; absent = HHS. Glucose and osmolality much higher in HHS. DKA = young T1 over hours; HHS = old T2 over days.
Clinical Features & Diagnosis
Clinical Features
  • Profound dehydration (often 100–220 mL/kg deficit — more severe than DKA): polyuria, polydipsia, dry mucous membranes, hypotension
  • Altered consciousness — directly proportional to osmolality; focal neurology/seizures (can mimic stroke)
  • Lethargy, nausea/vomiting
  • NO Kussmaul, NO ketotic breath — the bedside contrast with DKA
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Glucose >30 mmol/L
  • Osmolality >320 mOsm/kg
  • Ketones <3 / negative–trace
  • No significant acidosis (pH normal)

Osmolality formula: 2(Na⁺) + glucose + urea

Workup: U&E, FBC, CRP, cultures, ECG, troponin (silent MI), CT head if ↓GCS/focal signs

Precipitants
  • Infection (commonest), MI, high-dose steroids, glucose-rich IV fluids, new T2DM presentation
Management — Gentler than DKA
Key difference from DKA: fluids are the priority; insulin is secondary and cautious. Residual insulin + fluid correction does much of the work. These patients crash their glucose easily — over-rapid insulin causes dangerous osmotic shift.
Step 1 — IV Fluids (0.9% Saline) — The Mainstay0.5–1 L/hr — slower than DKA. Replace gradually over 24–48h. The deficit is huge but rapid shifts → cerebral oedema. Fluids alone often bring glucose down significantly.
↓
Step 2 — Insulin (cautious, only if significant ketones)Low rate (~0.05 units/kg/hr). Patients are insulin-sensitive — do NOT give full DKA-dose insulin. Only start if ketones present; otherwise fluids may be sufficient.
↓
Step 3 — VTE Prophylaxis (mandatory)Prophylactic LMWH for all HHS patients. Hyperviscosity + dehydration → very high thrombosis risk (MI, stroke, DVT/PE). This is unique to HHS and not required in DKA.
↓
Step 4 — Potassium (same rule as DKA)Insulin shifts K⁺ into cells. Check before each step. K⁺ >5.5 → none. K⁺ 3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L in fluids. K⁺ <3.5 → senior review.
Correct osmolality SLOWLY — rapid drop → cerebral oedema. Same "treat slowly" principle as DKA (glucose) and SIADH (sodium). Cross-ref both notes.
Complications
Thrombosis — The HHS Signature

Hyperviscosity + severe dehydration → MI, stroke, DVT, PE, arterial thrombosis. Higher mortality than DKA because of older, comorbid population. LMWH is mandatory — not optional.

Cerebral Oedema (Iatrogenic)

From over-rapid correction of glucose/osmolality. Headache, ↓GCS, irritability. Prevent by correcting slowly over 24–48h. Same mechanism as DKA — cross-ref.

Altered consciousness tracks osmolality. Osmolality = 2Na⁺ + glucose + urea. Correct slowly to avoid cerebral oedema.
No Kussmaul, no pear-drop breath — bedside contrast with DKA. pH and HCO₃⁻ normal.
