ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoglycaemia:
Overview — "Four is the Floor"
Hypoglycaemia = blood glucose <4.0 mmol/L. "Four is the floor." The fork: autonomic symptoms (early warning, <~3.3) → neuroglycopenic (brain starving, <~2.8) → seizure/coma. This is the rate-limiting risk of diabetes treatment — the reason HbA1c targets are relaxed to 53 (vs 48) once on ≥2 agents.
Counter-Regulatory Defence Cascade

As glucose falls: ↓insulin → ↑glucagon (first line) → ↑adrenaline (drives autonomic warning symptoms) → hours later: ↑cortisol + ↑GH. This sequence explains why symptoms come in two phases — adrenaline drives the warning; once defences are overwhelmed the brain is starved.

Aetiology
Diabetic Treatment (Commonest)
  • Insulin — too large a dose, wrong timing
  • Sulfonylureas — the oral agent that causes hypos; prolonged half-life → hypos can last hours/days (cross-ref Diabetes Treatments)
  • Precipitants: missed meals, exercise, alcohol, renal impairment (↓insulin clearance)
Non-Diabetic Causes
  • Insulinoma — β-cell tumour; ↑proinsulin:insulin ratio; cross-ref MEN1 (pancreatic tumours)
  • Alcohol — impairs gluconeogenesis; exaggerates insulin effect
  • Liver failure — no gluconeogenesis or glycogen stores
  • Addison's disease — cortisol deficiency → hypoglycaemia is a feature of adrenal crisis; cross-ref Addison's note
  • Sepsis, malnutrition, GH deficiency
Clinical Features — Two-Phase Sequence
PhaseThresholdMechanismSymptoms
Autonomic (warning)<~3.3 mmol/LAdrenaline / glucagon releaseSweating, shaking, hunger, anxiety, palpitations, nausea
Neuroglycopenic (brain starving)<~2.8 mmol/LInsufficient cerebral glucoseConfusion, visual change, weakness, dizziness, slurred speech, odd behaviour
SevereLower—Seizures, coma
Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness: recurrent hypos blunt the autonomic warning response — patients skip the warning phase and collapse without warning. β-blockers also mask the autonomic symptoms (sweating is preserved; other adrenergic signs are blocked). Classic SBA link.
Management — By Consciousness Level
Single decision: can the patient swallow safely?
Conscious + can swallow — Oral Fast-Acting Carbohydrate15–20g fast-acting carb: glucose tablets, GlucoGel/Dextrogel, fruit juice. Recheck glucose in 15 min — repeat if still <4. Then give long-acting carbohydrate (toast, biscuits) to prevent rebound drop.
↓
Unconscious / can't swallow (community) — IM GlucagonMobilises hepatic glycogen to release glucose. Works only if glycogen stores are adequate. Fails in: alcohol excess, liver failure, malnutrition, prolonged fast — no glycogen to release. In these patients: IV glucose is essential.
↓
Unconscious / can't swallow (hospital, IV access) — IV Glucose20% glucose IV via large vein (less tissue damage than 50%). Reliable regardless of glycogen stores — always works.
Glucagon Caveat

Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen — ineffective if no glycogen stores (alcohol excess, liver failure, malnutrition, prolonged fasting). Always give IV glucose in these patients instead.

Sulfonylurea Hypos — Admit

Sulfonylureas have a long half-life → hypos can recur for hours to days after apparent recovery. Always admit for observation and prolonged glucose monitoring. Do not discharge after a single correction.

After Recovery — Identify and Treat the Cause
  • Review insulin or sulfonylurea dose
  • Assess meal pattern, exercise, alcohol intake, renal function
  • Consider HbA1c target relaxation if recurrent hypos
  • Address impaired awareness: structured education, continuous glucose monitoring
Exam Pearls
"Four is the floor" — <4.0 mmol/L. Symptom sequence: autonomic warning (sweating/shaking/hunger) → neuroglycopenic (confusion/coma).
Commonest cause = insulin / sulfonylurea. Sulfonylurea hypos are prolonged (long half-life) → always admit and observe.
Impaired awareness from recurrent hypos blunts the warning phase. β-blockers mask autonomic symptoms — classic SBA trap.
Treatment ladder: oral carb (conscious) → IM glucagon (unconscious, community) → IV glucose (hospital / glucagon fails).
Glucagon fails in alcohol / liver failure / malnutrition — no glycogen stores. Give IV glucose instead.
Always give long-acting carb after fast-acting treatment to prevent rebound hypoglycaemia.
Non-diabetic causes: insulinoma (cross-ref MEN1), Addison's (cortisol deficiency), alcohol, liver failure.
HbA1c targets relaxed (to 53) once on ≥2 agents — hypoglycaemia risk is why. The rate-limiting constraint on tight control.

Overview
Core mechanism: Chronic hyperglycaemia → endothelial damage (leaky, non-regenerating vessels) + immune dysfunction (↑ infection risk)
Microvascular (glucose-driven)

The three -opathies — retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy

Lever: glycaemic control (HbA1c target)

Macrovascular (CV-risk-driven)

Atherosclerosis → IHD/MI, stroke, PAD

Lever: BP control, statin, smoking cessation

Overview — Agent Selection Framework
Framework: Pick agents by patient feature — not rote mechanism. The three axes that drive choice: hypoglycaemia risk · weight effect · special benefit/harm.
The incretin axis (anchors two drug classes): GLP-1 (gut hormone) → ↑insulin, ↓glucagon, slows gastric emptying, ↓appetite. DPP-4 breaks down GLP-1. So GLP-1 mimetics replace it; DPP-4 inhibitors preserve it — same pathway, two ways in.

Sulfonylureas + Insulin only — they force insulin release regardless of glucose level

Cause weight loss

GLP-1 mimetics + SGLT2 inhibitors — the obesity-friendly pair

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Complications:
Overview — The Biochemical Triad
DKA = life-threatening emergency. Biochemical triad: hyperglycaemia + ketonaemia + acidosis. This is the "no insulin → ketones" decompensation from the T1DM note. T2DM retains enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis → HHS instead. Cross-ref Acid-Base Balance (DKA = the textbook raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis).
Precipitants — "The I's"
  • Infection — commonest precipitant (sepsis drives counter-regulatory hormones)
  • Insulin omission / interruption — missed doses, pump failure
  • Intercurrent illness — MI, surgery, trauma
  • Initial presentation — first presentation of undiagnosed T1DM
Pathogenesis — Two Parallel Arms
Arm 1 — Glucose

No insulin → ↑gluconeogenesis / ↑glycogenolysis → hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → profound dehydration + electrolyte loss

Arm 2 — Ketones

No insulin → ↑lipolysis → free fatty acids → hepatic ketogenesis → acidic ketones → metabolic acidosis → vomiting → worsens dehydration

Both arms are accelerated by stress hormones (catecholamines, glucagon, cortisol). Vomiting from ketoacidosis worsens dehydration — a vicious cycle that kills if untreated.
Clinical Features
Dehydration (often 5–8L)
  • Sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, dry tongue
  • Hypotension, tachycardia, shock
  • Polyuria / polydipsia (osmotic diuresis)
GI / Respiratory
  • Vomiting, abdominal pain (can mimic surgical abdomen)
  • Kussmaul respiration — deep, rapid; blowing off CO₂ to compensate acidosis
  • Acetone breath (pear-drop smell)
Neurological
  • Lethargy, confusion
  • Impaired consciousness / coma in severe cases
  • Headache (early sign of cerebral oedema — a red flag)
Investigations — JBDS Diagnostic Criteria
Hyperglycaemia

Glucose >11 mmol/L (or known diabetic at any glucose if ketonaemia + acidosis present)

Ketonaemia

Blood ketones >3 mmol/L (finger-prick) or 2+ on urine dipstick

Acidosis

pH <7.3 and/or HCO₃⁻ <15 mmol/L — raised anion gap (ketones are the unmeasured anions)

The potassium paradox — the single most important investigation point:
Total body K⁺ is LOW (osmotic diuresis depletes it) but serum K⁺ is HIGH/normal on admission — because absent insulin lets K⁺ shift OUT of cells. Insulin treatment then drives K⁺ back in → serum K⁺ crashes → fatal arrhythmia if not pre-empted. This is why you check K⁺ before every step.
Other Investigations
  • U&E — urea/creatinine raised (dehydration); K⁺ as above
  • FBC, CRP, blood cultures — septic screen (infection is the commonest precipitant)
  • ECG — hyperkalaemia on admission; later hypokalaemia with treatment
  • Septic screen: MSU, CXR, wound swabs
Management — Fluids, Insulin, Potassium
The mantra: fluids first, then insulin, watch potassium. Two iatrogenic killers: (1) hypokalaemia from insulin driving K⁺ into cells; (2) cerebral oedema from over-rapid correction.
Step 1 — IV Fluids (0.9% Saline) — FIRSTAggressive rehydration — often 5–8L deficit. Start even if acidotic. Restores perfusion. Fluids before insulin — do NOT start insulin first.
↓
Step 2 — Fixed-Rate IV Insulin Infusion (0.1 units/kg/hr)Switches off ketogenesis. Continue long-acting background insulin; stop short-acting. Add 10% dextrose once glucose <14 mmol/L — keep insulin running to clear ketones (do NOT stop insulin to protect glucose).
↓
Step 3 — Potassium Replacement (per serum level)K⁺ >5.5 → none. K⁺ 3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L in fluids. K⁺ <3.5 → senior review; do NOT start insulin until K⁺ replaced (insulin will crash it further → fatal arrhythmia).
Iatrogenic Killer 1 — Hypokalaemia

Insulin drives K⁺ into cells → serum K⁺ crashes → fatal arrhythmia. Pre-empt: check K⁺ before starting insulin; replace if <3.5; reassess every 1–2h.

Iatrogenic Killer 2 — Cerebral Oedema

From over-rapid correction of glucose/osmolality. Headache + irritability + ↓GCS. Higher risk in young/children. Correct glucose slowly. Same principle as osmotic demyelination in SIADH.

Resolution Targets & Transition
  • Ketones <0.6 mmol/L, pH >7.3, HCO₃⁻ >15 = resolved
  • Transition to subcutaneous insulin — overlap with IV infusion by 30–60 min before stopping
  • Bicarbonate NOT routine — only pH <7.0 under senior guidance; risks paradoxical intracellular acidosis

HHS = marked hyperglycaemia + hyperosmolality + mild/no ketosis. The metabolic emergency of uncontrolled T2DM — often elderly, often previously undiagnosed. Residual insulin blocks ketogenesis. The two dangers: extreme osmolality → altered consciousness and hyperviscosity → thrombosis.

Step 4 — Potassium (same rule as DKA)Insulin shifts K⁺ into cells. Check before each step. K⁺ >5.5 → none. K⁺ 3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L in fluids. K⁺ <3.5 → senior review.
Correct osmolality SLOWLY — rapid drop → cerebral oedema. Same "treat slowly" principle as DKA (glucose) and SIADH (sodium). Cross-ref both notes.
Complications
Thrombosis — The HHS Signature

Hyperviscosity + severe dehydration → MI, stroke, DVT, PE, arterial thrombosis. Higher mortality than DKA because of older, comorbid population. LMWH is mandatory — not optional.

Cerebral Oedema (Iatrogenic)

From over-rapid correction of glucose/osmolality. Headache, ↓GCS, irritability. Prevent by correcting slowly over 24–48h. Same mechanism as DKA — cross-ref.

Exam Pearls
HHS = T2 emergency: insulin present → no ketones/acidosis, but glucose >30 + osmolality >320 over days.
The fork vs DKA: ketones/acidosis = DKA (T1, hours). No ketones/normal pH = HHS (T2, days). HHS has higher glucose + osmolality.
Fluids are the priority in HHS — cautious/low-dose insulin only if ketonaemic. Reverse emphasis from DKA.
VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) is mandatory — hyperviscosity → MI/stroke/DVT/PE. The HHS signature risk not shared by DKA.
Altered consciousness tracks osmolality. Osmolality = 2Na⁺ + glucose + urea. Correct slowly to avoid cerebral oedema.
No Kussmaul, no pear-drop breath — bedside contrast with DKA. pH and HCO₃⁻ normal.
Same potassium rule as DKA — insulin shifts K⁺ in; check before each step; replace if <3.5.
High mortality — older, comorbid population. Precipitants: infection (commonest), silent MI, steroids.
Overview — "Four is the Floor"
Hypoglycaemia = blood glucose <4.0 mmol/L. "Four is the floor." The fork: autonomic symptoms (early warning, <~3.3) → neuroglycopenic (brain starving, <~2.8) → seizure/coma. This is the rate-limiting risk of diabetes treatment — the reason HbA1c targets are relaxed to 53 (vs 48) once on ≥2 agents.
Counter-Regulatory Defence Cascade

As glucose falls: ↓insulin → ↑glucagon (first line) → ↑adrenaline (drives autonomic warning symptoms) → hours later: ↑cortisol + ↑GH. This sequence explains why symptoms come in two phases — adrenaline drives the warning; once defences are overwhelmed the brain is starved.

Aetiology
Diabetic Treatment (Commonest)
  • Insulin — too large a dose, wrong timing
  • Sulfonylureas — the oral agent that causes hypos; prolonged half-life → hypos can last hours/days (cross-ref Diabetes Treatments)
  • Precipitants: missed meals, exercise, alcohol, renal impairment (↓insulin clearance)
Non-Diabetic Causes
  • Insulinoma — β-cell tumour; ↑proinsulin:insulin ratio; cross-ref MEN1 (pancreatic tumours)
  • Alcohol — impairs gluconeogenesis; exaggerates insulin effect
  • Liver failure — no gluconeogenesis or glycogen stores
  • Addison's disease — cortisol deficiency → hypoglycaemia is a feature of adrenal crisis; cross-ref Addison's note
  • Sepsis, malnutrition, GH deficiency
Clinical Features — Two-Phase Sequence
PhaseThresholdMechanismSymptoms
Autonomic (warning)<~3.3 mmol/LAdrenaline / glucagon releaseSweating, shaking, hunger, anxiety, palpitations, nausea
Neuroglycopenic (brain starving)<~2.8 mmol/LInsufficient cerebral glucoseConfusion, visual change, weakness, dizziness, slurred speech, odd behaviour
SevereLower—Seizures, coma
Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness: recurrent hypos blunt the autonomic warning response — patients skip the warning phase and collapse without warning. β-blockers also mask the autonomic symptoms (sweating is preserved; other adrenergic signs are blocked). Classic SBA link.
Management — By Consciousness Level
Single decision: can the patient swallow safely?
Conscious + can swallow — Oral Fast-Acting Carbohydrate15–20g fast-acting carb: glucose tablets, GlucoGel/Dextrogel, fruit juice. Recheck glucose in 15 min — repeat if still <4. Then give long-acting carbohydrate (toast, biscuits) to prevent rebound drop.
↓
Unconscious / can't swallow (community) — IM GlucagonMobilises hepatic glycogen to release glucose. Works only if glycogen stores are adequate. Fails in: alcohol excess, liver failure, malnutrition, prolonged fast — no glycogen to release. In these patients: IV glucose is essential.
↓
Unconscious / can't swallow (hospital, IV access) — IV Glucose20% glucose IV via large vein (less tissue damage than 50%). Reliable regardless of glycogen stores — always works.
Glucagon Caveat

Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen — ineffective if no glycogen stores (alcohol excess, liver failure, malnutrition, prolonged fasting). Always give IV glucose in these patients instead.

Sulfonylurea Hypos — Admit

Sulfonylureas have a long half-life → hypos can recur for hours to days after apparent recovery. Always admit for observation and prolonged glucose monitoring. Do not discharge after a single correction.

After Recovery — Identify and Treat the Cause
  • Review insulin or sulfonylurea dose
  • Assess meal pattern, exercise, alcohol intake, renal function
  • Consider HbA1c target relaxation if recurrent hypos
  • Address impaired awareness: structured education, continuous glucose monitoring
Exam Pearls
"Four is the floor" — <4.0 mmol/L. Symptom sequence: autonomic warning (sweating/shaking/hunger) → neuroglycopenic (confusion/coma).
Commonest cause = insulin / sulfonylurea. Sulfonylurea hypos are prolonged (long half-life) → always admit and observe.
Impaired awareness from recurrent hypos blunts the warning phase. β-blockers mask autonomic symptoms — classic SBA trap.
Treatment ladder: oral carb (conscious) → IM glucagon (unconscious, community) → IV glucose (hospital / glucagon fails).
Glucagon fails in alcohol / liver failure / malnutrition — no glycogen stores. Give IV glucose instead.
Always give long-acting carb after fast-acting treatment to prevent rebound hypoglycaemia.

Fungal Infections in Diabetes Mellitus
Overview: Diabetes mellitus is one of the strongest risk factors for invasive and recurrent fungal infections. Both poor glycaemic control and the downstream immune defects converge to create a highly permissive environment for fungal proliferation.
Why Diabetics Are Susceptible
Mechanism Detail
Impaired neutrophil function Hyperglycaemia reduces neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and intracellular killing (oxidative burst)
Reduced complement activity Glycosylation of complement proteins diminishes opsonisation and fungal clearance
Impaired T-cell function Defective cell-mediated immunity reduces antifungal defences, especially important in mucosal candidiasis
High glucose as fungal substrate Glucose-rich secretions (saliva, urine, vaginal fluid) directly fuel Candida and other fungal growth
Peripheral vascular disease Poor tissue perfusion reduces delivery of immune cells and antifungal drugs to infected sites
Acidic environment in DKA Ketoacidosis impairs transferrin-mediated iron chelation → free iron available for Mucor growth

2. Mucormycosis (Zygomycosis) — HIGH YIELD
Mortality >50% if diagnosis or treatment is delayed. This is a medical and surgical emergency. Classic exam scenario: DKA patient with black nasal eschar and orbital signs.

Causative organisms: Rhizopus arrhizus (oryzae) (most common), Mucor spp., Lichtheimia spp. — order Mucorales ("bread mould fungi")

Classic risk triad: DKA + diabetes + immunosuppression (steroids, haematological malignancy, transplant)

Why DKA is uniquely permissive: Acidosis impairs neutrophil killing AND reduces transferrin iron-binding capacity → free serum iron becomes available as an essential fungal growth factor for Mucor species.

Clinical Form Frequency in Diabetics Features
Rhinocerebral Most common (~50% of all mucormycosis) Nasal sinuses → hard palate → orbit → cavernous sinus → brain
Pulmonary Haematological malignancy > diabetes Cavitating pneumonia, haemoptysis

Gastrointestinal Rare; neonates, malnutrition Bowel necrosis, perforation

Rhinocerebral Mucormycosis — Clinical Progression:

  1. Nasal/sinus stage: Nasal congestion, bloody discharge, facial pain, fever
  2. Palatal stage: Black eschar on hard palate or nasal septum (pathognomonic — do not debride without surgical prep)
  3. Orbital stage: Proptosis, periorbital oedema, ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI palsy), loss of vision
  4. Cerebral stage: Cavernous sinus thrombosis, altered consciousness, hemiplegia, death
Angioinvasion is the hallmark: Mucor invades blood vessel walls → vascular thrombosis → tissue ischaemia → black necrotic tissue. This explains the rapid, devastating spread and the black eschar.

Investigations:

  • CT sinuses + orbit + brain (with contrast): sinus opacification, bony erosion, orbital infiltration
  • MRI brain: cavernous sinus involvement, cerebral extension
  • Biopsy (gold standard): histology shows wide, non-septate (aseptate), ribbon-like hyphae branching at ~90° angles with vascular invasion and necrosis
  • Fungal culture: slow — do not wait for culture before treating

Hyphae Wide, non-septate (ribbon-like) Narrow, septate
Branching angle ~90° (right angle) ~45° (acute angle)
Classic setting DKA, diabetics Neutropenia, haematological malignancy

Treatment of Mucormycosis — Dual-pronged emergency approach:
  1. Surgical: Urgent, aggressive surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue (repeated if necessary). Orbital exenteration may be required to prevent cerebral spread.
  2. Medical: IV liposomal amphotericin B (preferred — less nephrotoxic than conventional amphotericin B), 5–10 mg/kg/day. Posaconazole or isavuconazole used as step-down or salvage therapy.
  3. Control the predisposing condition: Treat DKA, reverse immunosuppression where possible, optimise glycaemic control.

Note: Voriconazole (used for Aspergillus) has no activity against Mucor — a critical distinction.

Causative organisms: Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum spp.

Infection Site Clinical Significance in Diabetes Treatment
Tinea pedis Interdigital spaces of feet Portal of entry for bacterial cellulitis and diabetic foot infections — examine feet at every visit Topical terbinafine or clotrimazole × 2–4 weeks
Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) Nails (toenails > fingernails) Thickened, crumbling, discoloured nails — trauma risk in neuropathy; portal of entry for serious infection Oral terbinafine × 6 weeks (fingernail) or 12 weeks (toenail); amorolfine lacquer for mild cases

Diabetic foot care pearl: Tinea pedis in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease is a high-risk combination. The patient may not feel the interdigital maceration, which provides a route for Staphylococcus/Streptococcus entry and rapidly ascending cellulitis or necrotising fasciitis.

Causative organism: Cryptococcus neoformans (encapsulated yeast)

Less diabetic-specific; predominantly a disease of profound cell-mediated immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS CD4 <100, solid organ transplant). However, poorly controlled diabetics with additional immunosuppression (e.g. steroid use) may be at risk.

Key presentations: Cryptococcal meningitis (subacute; headache, fever, stiff neck), pulmonary cryptococcosis

Diagnosis: India ink stain (encapsulated yeast), serum/CSF cryptococcal antigen (CrAg), fungal culture

Treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine (induction) → fluconazole (consolidation/maintenance)

Euthyroid Goitre and Approach to the Neck Lump
Goitre = any enlargement of the thyroid gland, regardless of thyroid function. The majority of goitres in clinical practice are euthyroid — normal TFTs. Always assess: function (TFTs), morphology (USS), and cytology (FNA) when indicated.

Indications for Surgery (Thyroidectomy)
Operate when:

ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cancer:
Definition & The Core Concept

Thyroid cancer = malignancy arising from the thyroid gland. It usually presents as a thyroid nodule — but remember the vast majority of thyroid nodules are benign (only ~5% malignant) and most patients are euthyroid.

Four main types (+ thyroid lymphoma). The two “differentiated” cancers — papillary and follicular — arise from follicular cells, take up iodine, and have an excellent prognosis. Medullary and anaplastic behave very differently.
The Types
Type%Key factsSpread / prognosis
Papillary~80%Young (20–40s), female; radiation link; Orphan-Annie nuclei + psammoma bodiesLymphatic; excellent
Follicular~10%Older; cannot be diagnosed on FNA (needs histology for capsular/vascular invasion)Haematogenous (lung, bone); good
Medullary~5%Parafollicular C cells → calcitonin; ~25% familial (MEN 2, RET)Lymphatic/blood; intermediate
Anaplastic~1–2%Elderly; rapidly growing, locally invasive (hoarseness, stridor)Aggressive; very poor
✅ Differentiated (papillary & follicular)
  • From follicular cells; take up iodine and are TSH-dependent — hence radioiodine + TSH suppression work
  • Tumour marker for follow-up: thyroglobulin
  • Papillary spreads to lymph nodes; follicular spreads haematogenously
⚠️ Medullary & anaplastic
  • Medullary: secretes calcitonin (& CEA); associated with MEN 2A/2B (RET proto-oncogene); does not take up radioiodine
  • Anaplastic: elderly, undifferentiated, often unresectable; airway compromise; palliative
  • Also: thyroid lymphoma — arises in Hashimoto’s, rapidly enlarging
Risk Factors
☢️ Environmental
  • Ionising radiation — especially childhood exposure (e.g. Chernobyl) → papillary
  • Female sex; extremes of age (anaplastic in the elderly)
🧬 Genetic / associated
  • MEN 2A/2B (RET) → medullary
  • FAP / Gardner’s, Cowden syndrome
  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis → thyroid lymphoma
Clinical Features

Typically a painless thyroid nodule or neck lump in a euthyroid patient. Assess for red flags of malignancy:

🚩 Red flags
  • Rapidly growing, hard or fixed nodule
  • Hoarse voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement)
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Age <20 or >60; male sex; radiation or family history
🩺 Local / systemic
  • Dysphagia, stridor, hoarseness (local invasion — especially anaplastic)
  • Medullary: diarrhoea/flushing and features of a MEN syndrome
  • Usually normal thyroid function
Investigations
🔬 First-line
  • TFTs (usually normal)
  • Ultrasound neck — grades nodule risk (U/TIRADS); suspicious features: hypoechoic, microcalcification, irregular margins, taller-than-wide, ↑ vascularity
  • FNA cytology (Thy 1–5 classification) — the key diagnostic test
🎯 Type-specific
  • Follicular cancer cannot be diagnosed on FNA — needs excision biopsy/histology to show capsular or vascular invasion (distinguishes it from a follicular adenoma)
  • Medullary: calcitonin + CEA; RET genetic testing; screen for phaeochromocytoma before surgery
  • Staging CT/MRI for advanced disease
Management
✅ Differentiated (papillary/follicular)
  • Surgery: lobectomy (small, low-risk) or total thyroidectomy (larger/higher-risk) ± node dissection
  • Radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation of remnant/metastatic tissue in higher-risk disease
  • Levothyroxine — replacement and TSH suppression (TSH drives differentiated cancer)
  • Monitor thyroglobulin for recurrence
⚠️ Medullary / anaplastic
  • Medullary: total thyroidectomy + central node dissection; no radioiodine/TSH suppression; monitor calcitonin/CEA; genetics & prophylactic thyroidectomy in RET carriers
  • Anaplastic: usually palliative; secure the airway (tracheostomy), consider surgery/RT/chemo
  • Thyroid lymphoma: chemotherapy ± radiotherapy
Prognosis: papillary & follicular are excellent (>90% 10-year survival); medullary intermediate; anaplastic is dismal (survival often only months).
Exam Pearls
Papillary
Commonest, young patients, lymphatic spread, radiation link. Histology: Orphan-Annie nuclei + psammoma bodies. Best prognosis.
Follicular
Haematogenous spread (lung/bone). Cannot be diagnosed on FNA — needs histology to show capsular/vascular invasion.
Medullary
Parafollicular C cells → calcitonin (tumour marker); MEN 2 (RET). Screen for phaeochromocytoma BEFORE thyroid surgery.
Anaplastic
Elderly, rapidly growing, locally invasive, very poor prognosis; often palliative with airway management.
Most nodules are benign
~5% malignant; most patients euthyroid. FNA (Thy classification) is the key test.
Differentiated management
Total thyroidectomy + radioiodine + TSH-suppressive levothyroxine; follow thyroglobulin.
Lymphoma link
A rapidly enlarging thyroid on a background of Hashimoto’s → think thyroid lymphoma.
